Honestly, in almost every way I feel this is an improvement over the first game. The controls feel a lot better, rather than the super stiff feel of the first game you have a bit better air control & the game just feels smoother as a result. The game also has a bit of a visual upgrade & the music's pretty boppin' (though in terms of composition it may be a little monotonous? I remember the first game's OST being a bit more diverse than this one but ehh whatever.) I also like how the game expands upon the lore of the first game while also adding a lot of lore of its own.

And then there's the gameplay improvements. There's just a lot of little minor changes that really improve basic things - the hot springs being closer to the holy grail tablet, autosaving at boss ankhs, a lot more text space than the first game gave you (though i still switched to using screenshots preeeetty quick), and a bit more of a warmup period than the first game offered + a fairly straightforward first real area before the game really bares its fangs. And it still absolutely has a lot of what makes the first game good - though the puzzle design is decisively not as mean. Gone are puzzles where you solve something that opens a chest halfway across the ruins, and there's a lot more variety in general - fewer "break the wall" or "push the block" puzzles, a lot more lateral thinking. AT THE SAME TIME. Let it be known there is one puzzle that speaks of "incanted silence" that is missing a key element, namely mention of a "wheel". And there were two other points in the game I had to rely on outside info to make progress, though they were less egregious - one instance of a rather obtuse puzzle that requires use of one rather useless weapon & conveniently blocks off the single most important upgrade in the entire game. And another where you are either required to pay excessively good attention to room names or remember the location of a specific miniboss you fought dozens of hours ago to retrieve a very important key item. No other puzzle had me personally stuck for long periods of time & unlike the first game I was able to work out all the game's riddles and larger-scale puzzles on my own, which does feel really great, especially with how obtuse they could be in the first game. In general there's a definite improvement on that front.

In terms of the action side of the game, combat feels... okay. The entire set of secondary weapons is identical to the first game which is a bit disappointing, but they are almost all useful and most of them are required to solve puzzles at some point anyways. The primary weapons... look, you have two real valid options, the rest are all pretty much junk. And unfortunately one of those junk weapons is required for progress at one point (which is what had me stuck). The normal enemies feel... particularly annoying in places (those damn lokapala are demonic spiders from hell & a few enemies in some of the later areas are pretty painful to deal with as well) and the bosses are a huuuuge mixed bag, a few especially annoying minibosses (FENRIR.) and bosses that range from "appropriate for this point in the game", "too damn easy", "kind of a spammy garbage fest" or "awful garbage RNG instakill hellfest that still somehow isn't quite as bad as Viy from the first game" (Surtr can go to hell temple, ugh). Anyways it's not the primary focus for most of the game and you're given plenty of tools to mitigate boss frustrations in some cases so it's only a minor negative point and one I honestly expected.

The few problems this game does introduce are an excessive abundance of instakill "haha gotcha" traps (there are multiple crush traps in every single field) as well as the lack of spike invincibility (meaning have fun getting knocked back into spikes after an enemy hits you and taking even more damage). There's also one or two fields that have some.... questionable room design. At the same time the game feels like it has a better air of spectacle to it than the first game did, especially in a few key moments towards the late game, and I'll be damned if I wasn't super impressed when I figured out how the ruins were laid out and how clever it all was. 

The game as a whole is basically just more La-Mulana, but I mean, that's basically all I was asking for anyways. It improves a lot of issues the original had while still providing the challenge and amount of content you'd expect (I think it took me longer to beat this game than the first, though that was in part because I mostly avoided using a guide this time around whereas I used guides quite a bit in the first game - though even then I feel like I spent less time wandering aimlessly here.) I'm pretty satisfied overall and am already looking forward to a sequel in 5 more years or so (please?).

The La-Mulana series is an endlessly fascinating work of art. It subverts some of the most basic principles of game design and is so much better for it. 
Trying to give it a distinct genre is difficult. Many terms apply, but nothing really captures what the game is like. It is a metroidvania in the sense that you get more items and access to old areas, but a substantial amount of progression is tied to knowledge, not items. I'd say the game feels more like an adventure than any other game I've played, but that's still vague. 

The main gameplay loop is based on reading cryptic tablets with riddles on them, and determining where those riddles apply and how. The interesting thing is that these riddles are written almost like the password hint on your computer. Only intended to have meaning to the ones who wrote them. That's what makes it so rewarding. It often feels like the game itself is against you. That the game is not meant to be beaten. Giving up isn't letting yourself down, it's letting the game win.

It's easy to say that this game isn't for everyone, but I'd say that not everyone will see it to completion. It's alienating at every step of the way. However, if you are interested in video games as an art form you owe it to yourself to give this series a shot in order to see what can be done with the medium.

If you liked the first game, you'll like this one more. If you hated the first game, you'll hate this one less (but still hate it). My feeling is that this game contains everything that was good about the first game, with some good additions and less (but not none) of the frustrating parts.

Definite improvements:
+ The controls first and foremost. You can fully control your jumps now, and the double jump and wall cling powerups control more naturally. You still lose jump control if you fall off a ledge since that's crucial to the game's style of traps.
+ Pacing of the early game is much improved by making it slightly more linear. You can't leave the first area of the ruins until you solve its major puzzle and beat the first Guardian. Thus it can introduce and explain the game's core concepts at a more intentional pace.
+ Certain key information and items are given to you earlier, mostly due to the above. Particularly the teleport item comes early this time.
+ There's no items this time that can be lost forever, except maybe a few glossary entries.
+ The ruins feel more alive with an abundance of NPCs to talk to alongside the tablets, skeletons and shopkeepers. The various sages will even send you text messages as an extra vector for immediately-relevant information.
+ This game's plot feels less like you arrived after the important events and more like you are catalyzing them.
+ The new mantra system is brilliant, and used for many of the game's most satisfying puzzles. You now collect keywords and have to find instructions to chant specific combinations in specific places, or occasionally piece together clues to do so. It plays in well to the feel the game wants to evoke.
+ The areas are varied and have fun themes. This was already true in the first game, but the new game keeps invents new ones with only a few partial rehashes. For that matter the soundtrack is just as good as the first game.
+ Enemy and trap design is very good, with enemies maybe a bit more exciting than in the first game.

The mixed bag:
* Those NPCs also work against the game's puzzles. Some of them have multiple lines of dialog if you visit twice and a few even change their dialog as you advance the plot (which may have nothing to do with the puzzle they gave hints about). That means you have to keep talking to each one until they repeat themselves and you can STILL miss lesser hints in a way that just didn't happen in the first game.
* About 80% of the game's puzzles feel fair, and many make you feel very clever, but the ones that don't are real stinkers. So no difference from the first game. Many require moon logic, hinge on intuiting a fake or destructible wall, or have outright misleading hints. You will not finish this game without peeking at a guide many times.

Not so good:
- Boss design is... a mixed bag. There's some really good bosses, some complete pushovers and some horribly designed abominations. Fortunately one of the late game areas features a place you can pay 50 gold and have infinite ammo on all subweapons for a few minutes, which is enough to trivialize any boss that frustrates you. Definitely worse boss design than the first game.
- More than half your inventory is repeated wholesale from the first game, and I don't just mean the major gameplay-defining items. I mean minor trinkets like the "kill skeletons better" item and the "immune to bats" item. Other than replacing the keyblade with a better sword I don't think there's a single "new" weapon, though the rolling shuriken and spear got their trajectories replaced with much more useful ones.

[b]As the story goes[/b] you play as the daughter of the guy from the first game. You run across familiar characters on the surface with more 'modernised' looks, wearing casual clothes and using more up to date technology going from the box pcs in the first game and their software, to a laptop (some using tablets) and installing apps. That said, even if you skipped playing the first game and jump right into the second you don't have to worry about missing context because aside from saying their hellos and giving hints, they talk much about their old days beyond their role. As for the rest of the npcs, honestly its kind of neat running into the different races  that were thought extinct, just to hold a conversation with you in Eg-Lana (though adamantly, none of them want nothing to do with anything anymore so they are happy to just tell you their tale).

[b]Dungeon-wise[/b] its a hell of a lot more open, transitioning from the gate of guidance to the roots of yggdrasil, it's quite grandiose, the puzzles are well packed in the first few areas so it's pretty easy to just go it it blind and trying different things when something is out of reach. There is plenty of directions you can go in and a few ways to go about finding items (ex. first run through i went through niddhogg early and found the climbing claws, 2nd run through i got the ice cape first and swam trough the lava in that same area to get the claws from below). Might take a while to just stumble around since the areas are quite open but as long as you push in a direction every time you find a new item you really shouldn't get stuck.

That said, In both games there is a point when playing blind is no longer fun, in the first game it was when you got to the gate of illusion where the puzzles go from trial and error to actually needing to figure out the tablet hints (Wherever those might be). The 2nd game it's when you start to collect the later mantras (which honestly was a missed opportunity in the first game since you didn't really get to use those till the end, but is a cool idea for puzzle solving non the less). They are fine for a while until you need to play them in a certain order off vague hints, or need to play them in certain combinations with sparse hints to help. Thankfully you aren't really punished for just playing them randomly so there is that.

[b]Fight-wise[/b] as the movement got more smooth, the bosses got more intricate, there are even some cool mid bosses there to give you trouble, Some unique, some concepts reused (in that case if you played the first game, you'll know what you'll have to do). Though you might find some complaints about certain boss fights online, not sure if they were nerfed since, but i had fun fighting all of them, if one seems harder or more bs then just try a different approach, no matter how much you might want to just whip everything. 

[b]Some complaints[/b] If I had to pick some things, it would prolly be that everything runs off an invisible point system, the more you solve and collect things the more certain events progress, at some point the enemy count in areas double to triples to likely balance your power-ups. Unfortunately, when that happens can cause some really annoying blocks in some areas since they also inject harder versions of some enemies in places that were tame before. Going to the Ancient Chaos in my first play through for example i got completely mobbed because i couldn't figure out how to get there originally, 2nd play though i got there earlier and honestly felt refreshing not needing to take an hour to get to the grail due to enemy mobs anti-airing me into lava. 

Some triggers are wonky like the required event to get to Ixtab to appear. It took me far too long to figure out i had to go to the room in the roots where the squirrel mini-boss is since i already passed by that area much earlier and unlocked the short cut on the other side, so didn't occur to me to go back. That aside, everything else was either scripted based on progression chains or moved based on that invisible point system. 

The Eternal Prison is prolly the only other area that had me very on edge initially since its a no teleport zone upon entering, but after a while and getting to the grail point, turns out the area isn't that bad as long as you don't go through a red door, or if you do, have an idea of where a nearby blue door is to get out, Ended up being one the more simpler areas to go through despite the final boss puzzle (albeit frustrating due to the type of enemies you run into).

[b]All in all [/b] Older game but highly recommend if you just like puzzles and vania games. Consult a wiki if you get stuck and just enjoy collecting, fighting, and progressing.

If you have played the first game then you already know what to expect. If you haven't, then La-Mulana 2 is a hardcore metroidvania. Tricky platforming, fiendish traps, tough boss battles, and a giant labyrinth await you. The best part is that the solution to everything is given to you in the game, you just have to find said solution and make sense of it. It may be scrawled on a wall, it may be a mural, it may be a statue, etc. A lot of the clues are cryptic and it can take a lot of time to figure out what a clue means and what it pertains to. You will get frustrated, you will get lost, but if you persist it will be well worth it.

Sprawling metroidvania with many a complicated puzzle, like its predecessor. Often requires thinking outside the box. Mostly free of bullshit puzzles, although there are a few that probably aren't reasonable for even this series' demographic to figure out in a reasonable period of time. Learn to laugh at instant deathtraps, because you'll run into a lot (but mostly within only a couple of minutes of the last quicksave).

Hot tip: build a map of Eg-Lana as you go, taking copious notes, writing down every tablet, etc. I built a nearly-complete map of the game out of tiled screenshots, complete with the names of all the rooms, and it definitely makes solving a lot of the puzzles waaaay easier.

OVERVIEW:
La-Mulana 2 is a challenging Metroidvania that can be very punishingly difficult, and has a strong focus on puzzle-solving. The game has a charming visual quality and humor, while having a pretty great retro soundtrack. The difficulty in this game comes not just from the combat and platforming, but also from the puzzles - which are the primary appeal of this game. The puzzles in this game can be challenging, cryptic, and will require out-of-the-box thinking. However, finding the solutions to them is a highly satisfying reward. If this sounds interesting to you and you're fine with brutal difficulty, then this game is right for you and is a steal even at full price. 

DISCLAIMER:
Because this game has a strong focus on using your own ability to decipher and solve clues, it is strongly recommended to avoid trying to look up the solutions in a guide as that will spoil a lot of the enjoyment. I had to use a guide to get through the last major chunk of the 1st game, and it definitely diminished my fun. I played this one right after beating the first one and did my very best to avoid using a guide because I had a better idea of the challenge I was getting into. I managed to complete about 90% of the 2nd game without using a guide, and primarily used the guide just to make sure I had the items I needed to be able to complete the puzzle or not (so I wasn't wasting my time trying to solve an unsolvable puzzle) instead of using it to get the solution. Overall, I found myself enjoying this game more than the first, probably in part because I was much stricter with myself on trying to solve puzzles on my own without using a guide as a crutch. Despite my disclaimer, if you find yourself completely at a dead end, there is no shame in needing to use a guide for this game - it is very challenging - just do yourself a service and give it your best before you look up the solution to a puzzle.

PUZZLES:
The puzzles in this game are primarily presented to the player in the form of hint tablets that will start of with easy enough clues (use X item on this spot), but will eventually get much more cryptic later in the game. The puzzles at times will require at times for the player to even have to translate some of the text from the games's fictional language. There are many times where the player will be given many hints for a puzzle that will not even be able to be solved until much farther in the game, and will often time be referencing an area that is distant from where the hint was originally found. Because of this, it is STRONGLY advised to either keep a running text document/spread sheet, take physical notes, take screenshots through Steam, or a combination of all three. Otherwise, you will inevitably forget a crucial hint that is necessary for progression. I personally started off with screenshotting everything and deleting my screenshots when I was certain I no longer needed that hint as I already solved that puzzle. Even when I did this, I still at times would have well over 100 screenshots of "not yet solveable" hints. Plus, having to go through 100+ screenshots every time I wanted to reference a specific hint became cumbersome. I eventually started writing down and compiling hints that I knew were referencing the same puzzle. In retrospect, it would have probably worked best to do a combination of some screenshots while also keeping a running spreadsheet to make it easily searchable for certain keywords to easily find the hints that I was looking for.

COMPARISONS TO THE 1ST GAME:
Overall, I prefer the 2nd game to the first. While I prefer the more varied environments of the 1st game, I feel the overall flow, and pacing progression is better in the 2nd. The 2nd one has a lot more text, dialogue, and lore, which can slow things down and is a point against it compared to the pure gameplay experience of the 1st. The 2nd game has a lot more quality of life changes and actually features a tutorial of sorts that makes this game more accessible to new players, and is arguably a better starting point into the series instead of the 1st entry as a result. The 2nd game's puzzles felt easier to me in part because they were less cryptic, gave more pertinent information (e.g. references to locations), and the more cryptic clues were often closer to the puzzle they were referencing - instead of the 1st game sometimes having a cryptic hint that references doing a specific action in a specific place (that the hint didn't reference), at a location the player will not even discover for another 20 hours of game time. Also, the player has more control of the character's mid-air jump trajectory, so this game is definitely more forgiving and easier than the first on this matter.

Basically more of La-Mulana, which is what I wanted out of it.  The jumping is a bit more lenient, if that was an issue for you.  The puzzles in general are also a bit less obtuse, and there's no real instances of having to interact with the game in mysterious hitherto unused ways for certain puzzles.

I fully believe playing the first game is not required to play the second game. So this section is devoted to this game isolated from the first while a later section is comparative. La-Mulana 2 is an extremely puzzle heavy action-platformer (or metroidvania if you prefer). The game is lore heavy with a full unique mythos derived from a multitude of real mythos. The combat is largely functional, but difficult. Bosses are fought to collect key items and traverse further into Eg-Lana, the mysterious ruins. Enemies are mostly fought because they stand in the way of proceeding, but many can be avoided.

The game takes an interesting approach to difficulty. The game becomes more difficult with each boss defeated. Each step of difficulty adds more and stronger enemies to the entire game. Similarly, the game's hard mode increases the difficulty counter. Depending on playstyle, combat can be frustrating. La-Mulana 2 is a game about puzzles and bosses are no exception. Save points are plentiful and easy to access, so the many traps and difficult sections are easily retried. Additionally, boss fights are immediately retryable, meaning that fighting a boss multiple times is not very punishing.

The music and art direction of La-Mulana 2 are phenomanol. While I can't say each track is memorable, they all provide a strong atmosphere to the game. Every area has a strong visual direction. The Icefire Treetops have harsh reds and blues of fire and ice that stand out against its dark backgrounds. The Blood Corridor with its forboding imagery, dull colors, and chilling quiet. Every visual helps build an area's atmosphere from the color scheme to the wall, floor, and door design, as well as the types of characters within it and their history.

Now I'd like to compare the two games a bit. The largest improvement from La-Mulana 2 is the modified approach to puzzles. La-Mulana presents a huge amount of lore to the player to decipher to find solutions. In practice, it lead to many extremely vague and convoluted puzzles that would fail to brute force, trial and error, or players would just give up and look up the solution. La-Mulana 2 is much more willing to help the player. To my knowledge, there are far fewer tablets with much more useful information. The app for recording texts is also available from the start of the game and has no limit to the number of texts that can be recorded that I know of. This gives the player much more sufficient resources to solve even the more difficult puzzles. In this way, careful thought is valued over brute force. I do still think it would be nice to see NPCs like Xelpud or Mulbruk giving more contextual hints to discourage looking up answers online, but the game is very completable without outstide resources.

La-Mulana 2 runs in a modern widescreen resolution as opposed to the original's dated standard resolution. The jumping mechanic has been modified in a way that makes it much more reasonably forgiving. La-Mulana 2's jump feels restricted while La-Mulana's jump feels plain punishing. La-Mulana 2 is much more generous with item drops and early item availability as well. As mentioned prior, the text recording app is available from the outset. An item to view boss health is also available from the start. Coins are numerous from pots that drop many coins and subweapon ammo. The Holy Grail is very difficult to miss, unlike the original where the player could very easily miss one of the most helpful items in the game.

All in all, fantastic visuals, music, lore, and gameplay. Some feel it's a bit pricy, but if this type of game is your thing, then it's more than worth the price.

Four and a half years after a successful Kickstarter campaign, La-Mulana 2 has finally been released, and is proudly continuing the series’ tradition of just not fucking about. 

While a lot of modern Metroidvania titles tend to focus on combat, stats and gear, this series abides to one of my personal favourite philosophies of the genre. It treats the world like the most important character. Built around its own pace, every room feels like it was painstakingly designed with a unique and important function in mind, but to never sacrifice overall flow. Each new zone has a visual identity of its own, with a bangin soundtrack that injects a mad amount of energy to the game.

The player is expected to learn the intricacies of the ruins, understand the way it thinks. La-Mulana is filled to the brim with puzzles and secrets, all with different solutions and methods of approach. But it’s never unfair or overly abstract with these riddles. The game gives you everything you need to complete it, but nothing extra. A total lack of handholding, and a penchant for pushing the player to their next limit. Pretty much guaranteeing that every step of progress the player makes is their own. 

La-Mulana 2 does a good job at curving the difficulty in ways the original didn’t, making sure that you never feel totally in over your head. So long as you’re willing to get your hands dirty, take a lot of notes, think critically about every dead end you find, you can stay on top of the chaos. SO not for everybody, it’s a gruelling experience, but if a dickhead who forgets his twitter name every other day can do it, don’t shortsell yourself. I can’t name another game that feels anywhere near as rewarding. The absolute king of its niche just got an even better sequel.

I find the hardest thing about making a good hard game is making you feel accomplished by overcoming the obstacle the game puts in front of you. I can't say that La Mulana 2 succeeds in that every time, but more often than not, I am pumping my fist with joy when I solve that puzzle.

I went as far as I could without looking anything up, but near the end there are some pretty difficult puzzles. I am not ashamed to say that I looked up hints. Perhaps the game should be at a level where hints aren't needed, but I like the option to do so, as no game will be the same, and each player will find or miss things unique to them. The original La-Mulana is one of my personal favorites. It was challenging, it was fun, it drove me up the wall because of 
 the obtuse nature of the puzzles and  I had an absolute blast playing it. LM2 is exactly the same way except cranked up. The controls are a better finely tuned version of the "old school" type that the the 1st game had. The music was just as statisfying to listen to. The puzzles had maintained that level of hair tearing untill it all clicks and  the gameplay itself had that metroidvania of explore,solve, power up recipe that I love so very very much. 

Now lets go in to some depth of what I found in the game.
  
Those returning to the game will find a lot of callback to the first because refrences  to the first game are all over the place in thte first few areas of the game. Now this I found was a nice touch, but it did maybe come across as a double edged sword. There are a few times where you need to visit those areas and if you haven't played the first one then you may not understand the refrences and clues that tell you to do so.  This also brings up the second point that alot of the jokes and refrences that some of the NPCs give may fly over the head of those unfamilar with the game.  Does it make the game unplayable? Absolutley not it just may make it a bit confusing for those in the early game. or for those instances where you need to visit the areas.

That being said the level design itself I felt was excently done except for the last area which I felt needed a bit more polish for being the last area as it seemed a little to plain for being the last area. Those who played the original will know what i am talking about. 
 
Moving on the grapics and music are superb. Though i think the music in the first one was tad bit better. But they flow together nicely for the most part. I did experience some slow down in certain areas but I unsure if I should docks points or not as I'm unsure if it was a game problem or computer problem. I am willing to overlook however as it didn't really make it super slow more of an annoyance that quickly disappeared.

Gameplay wise while I would like to say it was phenomal there are a two issues I found that I had problems with(well three but the 3rd one seems more petty then anything else).  

The 1st issue is on how enemies flood the areas the more you go through the game. Now don't get me wrong I understand the premise of doing so. You explore and unseal more areas of the ruins and the enemies are able to get out of there areas into older ones thus making  the game  scale with your self and making older areas still a challenge. I get that and actually aprove of it. But the issue is some areas get flooded with so many enemies that becomes less a challenge and more a pain in the ass. Like I said I do understand why it was done.I just dont argee with how it was done in some areas. 

2nd issue is the boss encounters. In the 1st game the boss encounters I felt where the best part ofthe game.They made me feel like I was doing something epic (which i totally was) and were hard and often needed several tries to figure out how to approach them. This one...not so much. They ether seemed to tame in how they were done or had an almost broken feel to them. I did have fun fighting them but it felt less epic challenge of man vs god/monster or woman vs god/monster as it is in this case   and more mainstream "Meh I've seen better" reaction.

The 3rd issue Iam not really going to count as it seems rather petty then an actual issue. That is the fact that the sprint item makes you sprint but you cant stop without hitting a wall. My inner speed runner has problems with the fact that something that makes you fast is that uncontrollable. 

Anyway with all that said If you like the metroidvania type of game or if you liked the first game then go ahead and give this a go. However it is not for everyone as it is a harsh game and will not show mercy.

This game is like La-Mulana 1, but for normal people.

The riddles are streamlined. They no longer have this sadistic edge, that made you scream "AND HOW WAS I SUPPOSED TO KNOW THAT?" in the middle of the night. Most of the times when you see a riddle you have a decent idea how it would be solved, even if you dont have an item for it yet. Places for mantras are clearly marked, and hints for them are much more straightforward than before. You dont have to aimlessly reexplore the whole game after you did something — you can always directly see or at least predict results of your actions.

Levels remind the ones in original a lot. Egypt level with pyramids, greek level, weird level, tower level. What had changed is that levels lost their features. In original almost every level had rules radically changed. One level was pitch dark, forcing you to use flares all the time. Another level introduced slopes, and used them actively in it's puzzles. Another had frontside-backside switcheroo. Every time you find a new location, you could be sure something will surprise you. Unfortunately, Mulana 2 decided to mostly drop this idea. Levels are just levels. Many of them dont have a unique gameplay style (and even visual design barely changes). 

Level design, however, feels very thought out. Maybe even in a bad way. Someone seem to have spent a lot of time thinking how to fuck up the player in every single room they are in. Hero no longer has invulnerability after being hit, and that allows monsters to juggle you around. You slightly miss your jump, fall on the monster, damage knocks you on the spikes, spikes knock you on a different monster, who knocks you back on the spikes again. BAM, three quarters of your health are gone. Every time that happens (and it happens A LOT) I imagine some dev laughing maniacally.

Bosses are... mixed. The game introduces a lot of minibosses, 2-3 for each level at least. They are usually poorly designed, being very predictable and easily cheesed. At the same time, with some other bosses, I sometimes wondered if it is even possible to kill them with melee. The situation is very similar with guardians. They are visually striking, perfectly drawn and animated. Every single one of them is a pleasure to look at. However, some of them are piss easy, and some others seem to be impossible to kill, outside of few very specific ways.

La Mulana 2 is streamlined, casualized, simplified version of the original game. It is a response to all criticism for La-Mulana 1. Many of the hardcore fans will be disappointed. 

However, this is a game I can hope to actually finish on my own.

I didn't want to sit down and write a long review for this game like I did for La-Mulana 1 yet, but it felt wrong leaving it unreviewed. This game is the best entry point in the series, my favorite game in the series, and about as great a sequel as you could ask for. Cleans up a LOT of what I didn't like about the first game, and my notes were enough to get me through almost everything here. Game sounds awesome and looks pretty to boot; if you're interested I implore you to get this game. Also, the DLC is fantastic IMO, very funny and the scale (hehe) of the puzzles are refreshing,

If you thought the concept of the original La-Mulana's metroidvania design mixed with puzzles and riddles was appealing to you, but found the game overall too obtuse and frustrating to play, this game could be what you're looking for. Unlike the first game, I can see someone being able to finish this one without a guide. While I can't personally vouche for that as I had other games to (eventually) move on to, as befuddling as some of the puzzles got later on, I found that the game is much better at just giving you the clues to solve them. Alot of times, I'd check the hints I'd been given in hindsight and thought "Oh, this was actually pretty straight-forward." Not all the puzzle-design is tight and there were some distinctly La-Mulana 1 moments towards the end-half, but the fact that I actually got to feel clever by solving a good chunk of the game with the hints given and my intuition definitely felt better than in the original.

As well as that, I find the overall design of the game to be just better. It still has those La-Mulana staple "Gotcha" traps all over the place (In fact, it actually felt they'd been increased in quantity), but I overall found myself more engaged with the actual gameplay this time around. A boss fight was something to actually look forward to instead of begrudgingly accepting as they came and with the overall toning down of puzzles, I found myself having alot more fun traversing the levels than in the original.

That said, it's not an absolute step up from the original, as it does have issues of it's own. The first that come to mind are the technical ones. A game that looks like this shouldn't be having the amount of performance issues as it did, regardless of your PC's tech. From a design aspect as well, this game has a bit of a falloff-point in quality. Just about when you think you've hit a nice peak and are expecting the game to start winding down to a close, it just kinda keeps meandering for a few more hours. End-game pacing issues were something the original had as well, but not is that pre-final stage speed bump even worse than the original somehow, the overall design of the game gets increasingly more sloppy and unpolished by the end stretch. The puzzles start getting less rewarding to solve, rooms, traps and enemy design just start feeling hastily slapped together and this all culminates in a particularly frustrating and clumsy last area especially.

At this point though, a bit of pain and suffering feels like a part of the La-Mulana brand and if you're looking for a bit of a ballbuster that tests both your platforming and puzzle-solving skills, this one's not a bad place to look towards.

There's just nothing quite like La-Mulana, both the first game and this sequel. I'll never play another game like these two. I can't stand when game devs try to reinvent the wheel when they make their sequels and end up changing up too much, mostly for the worse, rather than leaving the stuff that everybody liked about the original the fuck alone. It plays the same as La-Mulana except with a bit more polish and finesse, the puzzle difficulty feels similar which I'm happy for since I felt they hit a good balance in their first game, it didn't need to be made easier or harder.
Some returning items have been given new uses to in conjunction with their old ones. Subweapons as a whole feel a lot more useful this time around. Hell, I've found myself using Caltrops and Rolling Shurikens on some midbosses to great effect. Guardians feel easier than the previous game IMO. So far anyway, I haven't finished yet. If anything changes I'll update this.
One thing I do like about the La-Mulana games is they always have a great variety of enemies per area and this game certainly keeps up that trend.
As for the all important music, well, I'd say it's not as consistently high tier compared to the original, there's more tracks peppered in that I'm not as keen on (and unfortunately they're usually played in the largest areas in the game) but the tracks which are great surpass anything in the original game. So basically, think of the originals ost as a straight line of quality with La-Mulana 2's ost both dipping below and above that line sporadically.

There's a good amount of game here too. Nothing pisses me off more than devs taking 5+ years to make a game, only for it to be easily finished in sub 5 hours. La-Mulana 2 will not be taking you 5 hours. Overall I am beyond pleased with this sequel. I was worried the difficulty would be lowered, but it's not. I was worried there wouldn't be enough content, but there's more than the original. When I played through the original La-Mulana, I gave it a negative review. I was put off by the lack of feedback that the game gives you, the poor controls, and some of the nonsensical puzzles. I’m happy to say that La-Mulana 2 improves on the first game in almost every way. 

The controls are better, the graphics are better, the puzzles generally make more sense and clues for them are organized in a way that makes knowing what area they reference possible. The music and visuals are overall still awesome. The game is definitely worth the $20 price tag. 

There are a few instances where puzzles are either translated badly or are just written in an overly cryptic way. But, unlike the first game, I don’t think it’s *impossible* to complete this game blind and with no help. Just unlikely. 

That being said, La-Mulana 2 is not for everyone. The game is very difficult. Some of the puzzles require you to think in a very abstract way, and progression will come to a halt many times, sometimes for hours. This game is built on punishing you for assuming it follows typical gaming conventions, and is extremely unforgiving to the unperceptive. I recommend bringing a notepad. I know I wouldn’t have gotten through the game if it wasn’t for the almost 50 pages of notes I took. 

--In Depth Rant Below-- Contains SPOILERS--

Everything I said above is true. I still recommend this game to those who want a deep challenge. That being said, this game can be absolute bullsh*t at times.

Why are the jumping controls still broken? Yes, they are better than in the first game, but they still just aren’t quite right. While in the first game it was somewhat forgivable because it was essentially a remake of an older game, and wanted to have the same mechanics, there really isn’t an excuse for it in this one. What it comes down to is not being able to control the direction you are falling. This is a staple in platformers and metroidvanias. The entire game is just less enjoyable than it could be because of this one frustration. I understand *why* the game functions in this way; they want you to fall into traps and take damage without being able to avoid spikes. I just don’t think it’s a good reason. The traps and pitfalls could be designed slightly differently so you still take damage, without the entire game being plagued by bad “falling controls”. 

The Gale Fibula item is the worst implementation of a dash I have ever seen in a game like this. When equipped, walking in a direction will cause the character to run in a straight line, completely uncontrollably, until they collide with a wall. In order to make use of it, you have to leave it unequipped and then only equip it for a few moments to use it, then unequip it again. Constantly being forced open the inventory and equip or unequip it really breaks the flow of of the game. Why couldn’t remain equipped and just be activated by a button press, or double tapping a direction, or just automatically activate after running in a straight line for long enough? This has been implemented better in almost every metroidvania I can think of.
Where was the quality control? On release this game was plagued with bugs, and the first patch to fix it actually broke the game further. I was about 90 hours in before I realized I couldn’t progress due to a boss respawning without a health bar and blocking my way. Even after most of these game breaking bugs were fixed, the game still crashes and enemies or items become randomly intangible from time to time. But, even worse than obvious game breaking bugs are the spelling, grammar, and translation errors on the clues. Good Lord this single issue almost made me quit the game. In a game like this, every word is cryptic and might contain clues and it is infuriating to realize that the clue you’ve been trying to decipher for hours is actually just a translation error or just something that the developers overlooked. 
An example of this is a clue that refers to “Naga” as the boss of an area. There is no “Naga” boss, and the clue actually refers to Jormungand. I assume that the boss was called “Naga” in an earlier build of the game and it was just an oversight, but this one clue “Naga seals the path to the virtual wise man” caused me to spend HOURS looking for an enemy named “Naga” because I thought it was essential in finding the “virtual wise man”. Please don’t think I’m nitpicking over one mistake. The game is RIDDLED (put intended?) with similar clues. Spelling and grammar errors, incorrect and inconsistent color coding of key words, or just clues that are so bizarre that even after completing the game I still don’t understand what they refer to, and I can only assume something was lost in translation. 
I don’t understand why the game was released like this. Most of these issues could have been solved within days if they simply had someone proofreading through these clues. And they *did* fix many of the problems within a few weeks of launch. I just feel like the game was rushed out and my enjoyment of it was tainted because of that. It’s really disappointing. I would have gladly waited another month for the game to be polished. 

The Brahma puzzle is absolute bullsh*t. There are a few puzzles in the game that I kind of rolled my eyes at, after spending hours trying to figure them out and in the end breaking down and looking at a guide. A lot of the time it’s something that “makes sense”, at least in the game’s internal logic, but is just so oddly worded in a clue that it’s easy to see why I didn’t understand it. But, the puzzles involving Brahma and the Yuga Wheels are absolute garbage. You start getting clues for this end-game puzzle very early on, meaning that the majority of my 100-hour playthrough was spent with me thinking about how to solve this puzzle. I finally looked at a guide when I realized that if I didn’t get it after 100 hours, I probably wasn’t going to get it at all. After reading the answer to the puzzle, *I still don’t understand it*. I must have spent an hour looking at all the related clues and the solution together, trying to reverse engineer how I was supposed to put together these things together in some kind of logical pattern to figure this out. Solving puzzles is supposed to be an “ah-hah!” moment. Someone telling you the solution to a puzzle you couldn’t figure out should elicit a “Oh, why didn’t I think of that!”. When learning the solution to a puzzle leaves you more confused than when you didn’t know the solution, there is a problem. 

Overall I felt like the last 5% of the game was really kind of rushed. The final area was uninteresting, short, and had almost no puzzles. The final puzzles involving the Seeress’s prophecy were kind of half-assed. You already know my opinion of the Brahma puzzle. The final bossfight wasn’t that difficult or as imaginative as the final bossfight of La-Mulana 1. And I was kind of disappointed at the lack of an ultimate puzzle. La-Mulana 1 had an amazing end-puzzle that took into account all the areas of the game and made you think hard about how everything fit together. La-Mulana 2’s ultimate endgame area puzzle was basically just using an item on 5 different doors. 

After everything though, I’m still looking forward to La-Mulana 3.

La-Mulana 2 is logical evolution of its predecessor - it's a metroidvania with more focus on solving puzzles than action, but don't think action is a cakewalk either. Lumisa, the new protagonist, controls better than her dad in the previous game, with more freedom of movement in the air, but still retains some inertia when jumping. Besides that and her ability to crouch and crawl, she has basically the same arsenal as her dad, starting with whip and getting various additional weapons and items. The game has some other small quality-of-life improvements, such as way more lenient behavior of fairies, or letting you have more than one software combination saved. Other than that, the heart of the game is still the same, you still have to deal with some [i]really[/i] difficult puzzles that will make you feel like a genius if you manage to figure them out yourself.

The presentation is a noticeable step up from the first game, though it also ties into my two main complaints. The OST is great, it has some really memorable tracks and it's at least on par with the original game's music, even taking my nostalgia into account. As for graphics, the improvements are really easy to notice. LM1 wasn't an ugly game, it had really well drawn sprites and backgrounds, and so does LM2, but switching from their own engine to Unity let the developers put some nice effects like reflections on shiny surfaces, and even lighting that most wouldn't expect in a 2D game. Now, I predict that quite a few of you reading this review shuddered at mention of Unity, engine whose bad fame is mostly undeserved, but I don't know how else to explain issues with performance other than devs not being used to this engine. My PC is not powerful, it's basically the same thing on which I first finished remake of LM1, but it still doesn't feel right to me to see slowdown in some areas, and from what I read in the forum people with stronger machines had greater performance impact than me, so that's rather odd. La-Mulana 2 is a worthy sucessor to the first game, but it shows some rough edges that will hopefully be adressed in future updates. It does improve some areas, but in others falls short.

[b] + Positives:[/b] 

+ Platforming and contronl over your character is much better than La-Mulana 1. You have much more control mid air and level design takes this in consideration. You can also grab from stairs during a jump. Can also crouch to evade stuff and use in puzzles. This is a big improvement over the rigid controls of the original.

+ Amazing character designs and artwork. NPCs now have superb portraits that add life to them.

+ More involved use of mantras. These were used only for the last puzzle of La Mulana 1 and now appear extensively across the whole game, in creative ways.

[b]= Some things remain closely the same:[/b] 

= Puzzles are still great in general. Although the balance is somewhat weird, as you have some really tough ones around the midgame, and the final ones are very obvious.

= Lore still great. The story told through the hints given by the tablets is still as well crafted and mysterious as in the original.

=/- Text saving still bad. The text saving limit was increased compared to the first game, but for this kind of game, that sometimes gives hints very early that are used very late, and with the added text from NPCs that also offer useful data, you will quickly hit the limit and find yourself taking screenshots or physical notes, which is an unneeded annoyance.

[b]- And some things have worsened:[/b] 

- Worse presentation in general. Bosses are much less creative in design, often mimicking the ones from La-Mulana 1 but with less inspired aspect and patterns. Levels often make use of photographs with lowered color count, which looks cheap and doesn't mesh well with the pixel art.

- Bosses are significantly easier, with less inspired patterns. They have low life even on Hard mode, so it's easy to speedkill them before they can do anything with certain tactics, or can be cheesed with secondary weapons. Save a couple of exceptions, they have few attacks that are very rigid and easy to avoid after you fight them a few times. They also have some hitbox issues, sometimes being very hard to hit with melee, but super easy with projectiles.

- Little invulnerability post hit leads to silly enemy+spike combos. This will be a deal breaker for many. In the original game, when you get hit you have full invincibility until you recover. This is no longer the case. Your invincibility runs very quick, so you'll find yourself getting juggled by multiple enemies or, much worse, falling into spikes for massive damage. So you could get hit by a tiny 5hp bullet, then fall on spikes for a lot of damage. You will curse a lot at this, especially because there are a lot more enemies on screen compared to the first game.

- Music still good but not as memorable. You'll probably enjoy it while you play, as it is by no means bad, but you'll soon forget it while you will remember themes like the Gate of Guidance or Tiamat boss battle for a long time.

- World design not as cohesive and unique among levels, most areas look samey. The first game has some of the best world building in any game, with the clever "front" and "back" sides of the ruins, each telling a different side of the story, and with a visual design that matched that story- You had the proud Giant statues from the Mausoleum, and the forgotten decayed corpses of the Graveyard. You had the bright, relatively friendly "tutorial" Gate of Guidance, and the ominous, twisted Gate of Illusion. Now areas loosely follow the culture they belong to, but without the level of finesse and detail of La Mulana 1.

- Translation is wonky. Some hints are unclear and make certain puzzles harder, and seems to be more a translation problem than the developer's fault. Also, for some reason everyone talks super casually and swears a lot. I don't know if this was in the Japanese text, but the first La Mulana wasn't like this, and doesn't look good now.

- Lots of bugs as of now. Another problematic point if you want to play the game right now. I personally haven't run into many serious bugs, but the bug report thread on the forums is quite big and some people even got some save ruining ones. You should be fine if you make use of all 15 save slots, but you might also wait until a patch or two solve the major bugs the game has right now.

- Anticlimatic ending: while the game gets progressively tougher, with some puzzles even surpassing the fiercest of those on the predecessor in complexity and difficulty, the final puzzle hold your hand, the final area is a rehash of the secret level of La-Mulana 1, the final boss laughably easy, and the final sequence completely lacks any tension. While it doesn't ruin the game, it looks rushed and detracts a bit from the overall experience.

In short, the game is good, but feels like it needed a few more months in development to be fully polished. Most of the issues will most likely be ironed out on future updates to improve the experience. If you liked the first game, go for this one. If you love tough puzzles, go for it too. La Mulana is an experience like no other, and this sequiel manages to give us more of that, at a good level of quality despite its problems.

[h1]"Would you like to hear that again?"[/h1]

I never make serious reviews for videogames, but if I had to choose a game for one, this would be it.

La-Mulana 2 takes everything that makes La-Mulana 1 a special and unique experience and cranks it up to eleven, while adding its own flavour to it and proposing easier controls than the first game. This is the perfect sequel and everything a sequel should be for a videogame.

This review is pointed at people who finished La-Mulana 1 already and want to try this sequel.

[h2]What makes La-Mulana special?[/h2]

What makes this series beautiful and special is that these games don't really care if you finish them or not by yourself, these are created to challenge people's attention to detail, power of will, patience and cunning like no other game in the world does, and if you don't have what it takes, that's on you. This also reflects into the feeling of the game world: the ruins you are exploring do not like you and they are trying to get you outside in every way possible. The usage of some sort of external help is definitely normal and expected, but it's up to you to decide when you can't progress by yourself anymore. This is the player's ultimate test.

I love when videogames reward my attention to detail, but to be very honest, almost every time my attention to detail is not actually necessary, it's usually just a nice little bonus in the form of a reward or easter egg.

But no, these games demand a lot from the player, you are *expected* to put your absolute everything into them and chances are that even if you do put your absolute best, you will fail.

This doesn't mean these games don't give you all the tools necessary to finish it. Matter of fact, they do and they do it spectacularly. It's up to you to connect the dots at all times.

[h2]What does La-Mulana 2 improve over the previous entry?[/h2]

A lot of the jank that you can experience in La-Mulana 1 is gone, and while I don't think the first game's controls are bad or worse, this new entry did decide to allow for easier movement and more freedom. A lot of QOL and streamlining was added. For example, while in La-Mulana 1 it was often necessary to explore areas multiple times as the world changed without you really realizing, this is no longer the case: if any change happens in the world, it always makes sense and it's understandable. Main bosses will have a checkpoint before the fight starts, so you don't have to walk all the way back to the boss each attempt. Software combos are actually explained in the game somewhere.

The OSTs are absolutely incredible as usual, of course, and the boss fights are vastly improved over the first game - they're not perfect but they're definitely more fun in my opinion.

Overall, I'd say the puzzles are just as good if not better than the first game, and in my opinion they're also harder, but usually less cryptic.

I strongly suggest taking notes (pictures of tablets included, those can and will be very useful), it really changed the experience for me. I have also created a map of the entire game with screenshots, but I'd say that's not necessary at all.

[h2]Conclusions[/h2]

This game stole the number one spot of my favourite games ever from Outer Wilds. Not because it's necessarily better, but it gave me exactly what I look for when I play a videogame and allowed me to test all my skills as a player in a way no other game would be able to.

If you liked La-Mulana 1, this is a MUST play.

I was extremely impressed by La-Mulana 2. You should give it a try if you were at all excited by its predecessor La-Mulana, even if you eventually wound up turned off my LM1's more obscure or arbitrary puzzles. 

If you have not played La-Mulana (either the original or 2011 remake), it's still quite reasonable to start with this game. However, before starting either game you should be made aware that La-Mulana is in some ways unlike most games in that it very much expects you to pay attention to things, even things that appear to be "in the background" or "useless lore" at the time you read them, and to take good notes. Not doing this will likely lead to a lot of aimless wandering around and general frustration.

I have played only the 2011 remake of the original game. LM2 felt like a true sequel to that game, retaining most of the feel while cutting out exactly the parts that bothered me most about the original. Namely, the puzzles in LM2 are siginificantly better clued, with almost no puzzles where the solution seemed arbitrary or deducible from tablet text "only in hindsight". At the same time, the puzzles that were here were a bunch of fun, ranging from the simple one-room "cleverly interpret the tablet in this room" to the world-spanning "have you paid enough attention to the lore and layout of these ruins to be able to put together what you're supposed to do here". 

I will try to also make note of my biggest complaints, to round out the review:
[list]
[*]Occasionally during my playthrough I encountered a few bugs, and there was at least one game-breaking bug I know of that has since been fixed. Given that La-Mulana is a game about "noticing weirdness" and often requires interacting with the game in creative ways, it can often be difficult to distinguish a bug from a puzzle. This leads to a lot of frustration for people not willing to look things up. 
[*]Related to the above, it seems to currently be possible to softlock your game at various points and need to restart from the beginning if you don't have an appropriate backup save. (My advice is to make liberal use of the various save slots. This kind of softlock would have happened to me at least twice during my playthrough had I not been keeping a good set of backup saves, as far as I can tell.)
[*]My hand was held a bit more than I would have liked during a few major, world-spanning endgame puzzles. Given that there were other puzzles I found extremely difficult, it's not unlikely that I just happened to be randomly keyed in to some things and totally oblivious on others, and that other people will have a different experience.
[*]There is one lategame puzzle that appears to from a translation error, making its solution (as far as I can tell) not deducible from in-game clues. Hopefully this will be fixed in a future update. (This is a small problem if you are willing to look up solutions to puzzles on which you get stuck. But I find that having a strong "no-hint" policy is good for La-Mulana in general, since the game is very open-ended and often the thing you think you are stuck on is not actually the thing you need to do, in which case "looking up the solution" often winds up spoiling a large chunk of the game. This means that even one not-enough-information-provided puzzle, while an understandable mistake from such a small team working to localize into many different languages, can unfortunately cause many hours of fruitless wandering!)
[/list]

This game is [b]the Metroidvania to end all Metroidvanias[/b].

DIFFICULTY - The puzzles can get insanely hard. You won't exactly be asked to solve differential equations, but you will need to recall clues on the other side of the map from 10 hours ago to make solve some of them. The good news is there is actually an in-game 'app' to store most of these clues for you. You will feel like a crafty melon-farmer. Some will probably turn out to be too much for you ([i]...idiot :3[/i]), but there is a dedicated wiki that can get you out of any jam. Said puzzles rely on pattern-matching, noticing missing objects, paying attention to the historical context provided by the various NPC-s, and solving riddles. While I really enjoyed the difficulty (thinking about these puzzles became my only excuse to stop playing), others might not. You do you.

The platforming and combat are equally challenging. The platforming in particular is punative: The character stops on a dime, which is frustrating and takes getting used to. There is no forward momentum when the character is jumping forward, either. There are also TONS of absolutely hilarious traps that you will not see coming. You will not be angry about the creativity of some of them. Others will frustrate. You will learn your lesson and keep coming back for more though.

MUSIC ~ The music isn't inspired imo, and there is one level in particular that will make you want to tear your ears off your head (or put on a podcast instead). The rest of it is at worst ok though.

GRAPHICS ~ The levels feature beautiful ascended PlayStation-era pixel art, but the best part of the game are the painted and animated NPC's. The totality of this experience convinced me to call the the Graphics a "MASTERPIECE"

A fun, overall well made, and [b]difficult[/b] adventure game with a good amount of content, it took me weeks to beat it.

The primary difficulty of course comes from solving puzzles that will bust your brain trying to figure them out for yourself, and yet it's very doable to beat it blind if you keep an open mind and [b]plenty[/b] of notes [b]at all times[/b], even when you don't have enough space in-game to keep all your notes.  I managed to beat the [i]overwhelming[/i] majority of the game blind, with only a small outside hint when I got stuck somewhere and then later on I needed to look up a solution to another puzzle more thoroughly (even though it was something I should have figured out for myself looking back on it), but that was all the outside help I needed, everything else I managed to figure out blind and it was pretty satisfying overall.

There were definitely times that I got frustrated about being stuck for a while though, and I got stuck on [u]quite a few[/u] things which became a drag in some parts, so if you don't want to play a game where you'll likely get stuck often and/or you don't want to play a game that requires patience to play it blind then this probably isn't the right game to play, although if you're fine with looking up solutions to puzzles frequently then it's still probably a fun game to play through even with outside help.

That said, this game does set itself apart from the previous game by making the vast majority of its puzzles far less cryptic and obscure.  I believe that some people liked the way La Mulana 1 handled its puzzles and don't like the "casualized" sequel quite as much as a result, but I still found La Mulana 2 to be [u]plenty[/u] challenging to beat and I wouldn't change much in that regard.  I also played through La Mulana 1 as well with its cryptic & obscure puzzles, and even considering I could have played that game more intelligently--mainly I didn't keep my own set of notes for La Mulana 1 which bit me in the ass hard and I regretted that a lot--I [i]still[/i] thought (and continue to think) that a lot of the puzzles were overdone in that game.

In particular, the most notable difference with La Mulana 2 is that when you solve a puzzle you see the results immediately in the same room the [i]vast[/i] majority of the time, and the very few times where that's not the case then it's a puzzle where it's very obvious what you did and why; this is almost the complete opposite in La Mulana 1 where just pressing a switch could send you to an entirely different area (or even a different zone) to find out what you accomplished.  (It's not really so surprising, then, that I had to look up a guide pretty much constantly after a certain point in La Mulana 1, which really killed my enjoyment of the game [i]drastically[/i].)

Considering the difference, I found La Mulana 2 to be a lot more fun (even if still a bit frustrating at times) because of that and I think the developers did a good job toning down the cryptic & obscure puzzles in the sequel while still making it quite challenging.  I will admit that I was [i]slightly[/i] disappointed that some other puzzle elements and conventions were not retained from La Mulana 1, presumably in order to streamline the sequel a bit more, but that shouldn't really discourage anybody except the most diehard original La Mulana fans, and they probably don't need to read this review anyways.

One criticism that I have of this game (and its predecessor too) is that even though there's a perfectly fine system for keeping various notes and messages in-game, it becomes clear [i]very[/i] quickly that there's not [i]nearly[/i] enough capacity in-game to keep all the various notes that you need to write down, simply due to the sheer volume of things you need to be able to refer to at any given time.  I understand if the limitation is intentional (which I'm pretty sure it is) and I'm not griping about needing to write down some of my own notes at all, but after a point it became a monumental task just to type out notes from in-game to a text file (let alone organize my notes well enough) because of how much there is to keep note of and how long it can take before some of those notes finally become irrelevant.  If there was just more capacity for in-game notes to be kept around it would have been less of a problem, and I personally think that there should be [i]at least[/i] 2x as much capacity for in-game notes to make it less tedious and annoying to manage the endless amount of notes.

Everything said and done though I thought it was definitely worth ~$20 and I'd definitely like to see more games like this.

Okay! Let's begin:

The first game was a rather unique take on the Metroidvania subset of 2D platformers. It was big, complex, full of retro charm, and difficult enough that it didn't care one bit whether the average player would ever see the staff roll or not. It was a bold experiment by a small Japanese indie team obsessed with the old MSX 8-bit system, and I found it utterly fascinating. The WiiWare remake of 2012 -the version I played first- was one of my favorite games of that year.

La-Mulana 2 is... essentially the same game, with a new coat of paint.

Let's start from the beginning. La-Mulana (and, by extension, La-Mulana 2) is heavily based on an old MSX game by Konami called "The Maze of Galious". The tiny character sprites, the way the game world is structured, the general gameplay mechanics, the character movement and jumping physics, it all bears heavy influences from that game. This is particularly true in the original release, which featured 8-bit graphics and sound design that mirrored those the MSX was capable of.

Now, La-Mulana is a pretty difficult game, especially if you go in blind. However, even though there sure is a learning curve to navigating the platform-heavy, enemy-infested ruins, what really defines La-Mulana's difficulty actually resides in an entirely different aspect of the game: the riddles.

80% of the game consists in figuring out complex riddles and puzzles (most of them mandatory) in order to progress, with minimal to no hand-holding whatsoever. Usually, the hints for solving these riddles are located in entirely different areas, and further obscured by intentionally cryptic wording. It's the kind of game that requires comprehensive documenting of practically everything. To stand the slightest chance at beating the game blind, you pretty much have to draw your own maps and take notes of every single tablet and NPC dialogue you come across, as well as having a sharp eye for subtle details and the brains to juggle it all. And even then, you're not guaranteed to make it to the end without looking up the solution to a riddle or two here and there! It's a very demanding game in that respect.

Now, everything I said so far about the first game applies to La-Mulana 2 as well. And I mean everything. If you played the original, then you know exactly what to expect here. This sequel is essentially the first game, but set on a new set of ruins, with a couple other changes and embellishments here and there. But the foundation and design philosophy of the game remain exactly the same as in La-Mulana 1. Whether that is a good or a bad thing, that depends entirely on you and what you want from this sequel. I will say this, though. When over half of the inventory is the same as the first game's, and even a few bosses and scenarios are pretty much lifted wholesale from La-Mulana 1 with minimal alterations, then a case can be made that perhaps things may be a bit too "samey" for their own good at times.

That aside, there's still a lot of fun to be had here, because La-Mulana 2 is legitimately a good game in its own right. Sure, there were some bugs and softlocks at release, but the worst ones have already been patched out, and the rest are surely to follow suit soon. The devs appear to be quite active on that front, which is very much appreciated.

With all that said, if you haven't played the first game, I'd suggest you give that one a try first. Then you can decide whether you also want to play this sequel or not. Also, there's the fact that La-Mulana 2 spoils pretty much the entire plot of the first game in the first fifteen minutes or so, so that's something else you may want to consider, depending on how much you care about video game plots.

So, in closing, I give this game a solid recommendation... provided you are the kind of hardcore retro-gamer this game was made for, of course!

I played La-Mulana 1 almost guideless. It was pain and suffering.
I played La-Mulana 2 a bit less guideless. It was still pain and suffering.
The moments inbetween the pain and suffering are so worth it though.
I did not come across game-breaking bugs during my playthrough.

Regarding my recommendation:
If you played the first La-Mulana and still got it in you, I definitely recommend this one.
This game's literally just more of what the first one was, but with some quality of life features added. (In particular, the platforming controls are a lot less strict in this one.)

However, if you are a newcomer to the series, it's a bit more complicated.
First off, you *can* go for this game. Sure. But since this is a sequel to the first game, both lore-wise and mechanically, you may want to consider going for La-Mulana 1 first.
It's essentially the same experience. And especially if you're still on the fence about the series, going for the first game might end up saving you a few bucks for now, in case you don't like it.

If you are into the idea of feeling smart for solving cryptic riddles, and also have enough resiliance to not get immediately discouraged by the sight of a Game Over screen (or... hundreds, for that matter), give this series a try.

Be advised that this game requires a decent amount of brain juice to complete. And a lot of note taking. Perhaps even an external image editing tool to stitch screenshots together.
Ya gotta *earn* that victory.


Thing is, La-Mulana hates its player. (In more ways than one.) This game does *not* want you to win just like that.
But it also doesn't want to be *unwinnable*. And that's a weird balancing act right there, as you may notice yourself when playing the game.

There are hundreds of tablets with extremely cryptic hints written on them, scattered all throughout the ruins. Also, there are hundreds of secrets hidden all around the ruins. It's your job to figure out which tablet relates to which secret, and how to uncover that secret in the first place.

As these riddles can be a bit *too* cryptic every now and then, I'd recommend setting yourself a personal limit as to how far you are willing to push yourself for that sweet, sweet satisfaction of progression.

Lots of people take pride in blind, "guideless" runs. That is, they never look up *anything* about the game and solve every single riddle on their own.
In theory, that's the intended way of playing the game, and it leads to the most satisfaction in the long run.
But it also leads to a *LOT* of dead air, during which you're just... frustrated. And annoyed. And hate everything.

So whenever I'd find myself having run in circles for an hour or two, to save myself some time, I'd resort to the hint-based guide. (You can find it in the Community Hub for this game.)
Doing it that way, you at least get a "nudge" in the right direction, which can significantly decrease the amount of time spent wandering, without taking away *too* much from the riddle-solving aspect.

It's all about balance. Because sometimes, the whole game becomes much more enjoyable if you *don't* end up wandering aimlessly for 10 hours.
But on the other hand, if you spoil every riddle, you also spoil yourself the satisfaction you get from *solving* those riddles. And you may as well not have bought this game in the first place.
It's up to you.


As for me, if they were to ever make a La-Mulana 3, I'd sign up for it again. There just isn't anything else like this series that I know of. Truly legendary stuff.
