La Mulana 2 is the sequel to the remake of La Mulana 1. Its a large map indie metroidvania themed around ancient ruins and rings fondly of Metroid 3/Castlevaina SOTN but with a uniquely non-linear map, and (sometimes) extremely complex puzzles. What makes La Mulana so incredibly satisfying and unique is the game's very liberal approach to puzzles. Veteran's of the first title may be a bit better prepared on what to expect, but the magic of the game lies in the way the developer approached these puzzles (and traps.) La Mulana 2 distinguishes itself from other games of it's genre by creating a punishing and vast world where literally anything can happen. Puzzles sometimes require very unorthodox solutions, and I think this is when everything shines brightest, in it's pursuit of forcing the player to think critically and analytically to solve the games myraid puzzles.

First let me state: I love this game, and devoted many hours to it. There are some gamers here who play many games many more hours than I do, but in my 25 years experince gaming, this game is one of a bespoke few I've ever been so engaged with and enthusiastic about seeing through to the end. Excluding the ending, which I will elaborate on below, I would argue this game is so excellent in almost everything it does that it comes just short of being genre defining. No 2 puzzles are the same, and this game is HUGE. It's almost impossible to guage how far you are in the game, and for each door you open, 3 more lie behind it. The game has amazing potential for speedrunning and sequence breaking, as the event trigger system is somewhat forgiving, yet robust, preventing many (but not all) potential softlocks from exploring out of order. Combat is sometimes frustrating, but I believe that it is a game design choice, not a bug. You could compare the early game to, and please no cringing: Dark Souls, in that the player needs to enter a new area and find a save point before they can safely start exploring each new area. Plus, some traps are unfair, but you generally won't fall for the same trap twice unless you aren't paying attention. In the early game, your jumps must be deliberate and timed, and your melee attacks need to be defensive and intentional As you advance, your character becomes much more powerful, giving combat encounters a more arcade-styled feeling. I would say that this evolving gameplay made me feel as if I was getting more powerful and gave combat a nice flow as things sped up and as I gained new items.  I believe that this was an excellent game design choice. 

My first complete playthrough took me 76 hours, and I needed to look at a guide a few times to help me along at the end, as sometimes the game is not explicitly clear about it's intended path forward for you.  This is one of the game's greatest strengths but sadly also a weakness. As the player approaches the endgame, puzzles start to become [i] very [/i] complex and obscure. The game requires the player to cut about the entire map on guesses of where the trigger might be, as the in game reference map is quite simple. By the end, you will know this map quite well and have no problem navigating it, but at the beginning of the game the amount of paths you have open to you are at times, overwhelming. Strangely, the end of the game feels just the opposite: you'll feel as if you've lifted every stone and looked in every room, pulling your hair out trying to solve the last few puzzles. Compounding this, there are a few examples of some poorly translated clues that can cause a player to lose confidence in the game's way of accurately conveying hints. I only encountered this to negative effect once, and it's easy enough to figure out, but these are things that will hopefully be ironed out in future patches. This game is complexly coded in the way triggers work, so it is understandable that some bugs are present. 

Almost all of these bugs I mentioned above are in the late game, which brings me to my greatest complaint, the ending. The last 20% of the game has a noticible spike in difficulty of puzzles, while strangely getting easier in terms of action. The creatures seem less aggressive and more buggy, while the puzzles are cryptic and time consuming. One end game puzzle is even so complicated you'll probably spend more time on it than all of the other puzzles in the game combined (it's a doozy). As the player proceeds to the final acts before the end area, you'll notice that one specific area becomes completly inaccessible because it's only entrance is permanently blocked by a late game event that must be deliberately triggered. If the player had not gotten a (not very obvious) trigger here with a specific item beforehand, a puzzle required for finishing the game will not be able to be completed. If the player is only using one save file, yes, this will force you to start the entire game over- I'll admit that this is pretty bad. This actually happened to me, but I fortunately had a backup shortly before, just in case. I lost about 30 minutes of gameplay that I quickly made up. Please practice due dilligence: I recommend liberal use of the games multiple save slots to ensure if something does break, you'll at least be able to shift to an earlier save.

As for the final area of the game, it is very clearly rushed. There's no point in even going into specific rooms or choices of enemies, etc- anyone who played up to that point experiencing the lush and full map Nigoro gave us solving the same puzzles I did etc etc, there's absolutley no way you wouldn't notice the almost freefall drop in quality the player experiences in this final area. No mechanics, skippable bosses placed with no attention to reason or lore, and a final boss so dissapointing that I recommend just playing up until opening the final gate and just enjoying the game for what it was up to that point.

I would describe the first 96% of La Mulana 2 as a superb work of art that pushes metroidvanias further, and entertains for hours, it gives a great rewarding feeling when you finally solve tricky puzzles, you can tell every piece of this 96% was lovingly crafted.

But.

That last 4% is absurdly complex puzzles followed by the most absolutley lack luster final area and final boss. It feels like it was accidentally shipped with the last area still in alpha. ------

These complaints are entirely localized to the ending. If you can see past this problem, I would actually say La Mulana 2 is a work of art, and a rareform example of true vision in game design, and passion for a project that sadly got forced out too soon. You could sit down and play this game for 50 hours right now, and you would still not be at the content that would start slipping in quality. The only "bad" part is the very final area. About 30 minutes of a 75+ hour game. So with all this said, this game is highly recommended. I say that every rose has it's thorns, and La Mulana 2 is a masterpiece despite a small mistake at the end.

First I have to say that the sprites art is even better than the first game. Each NPC gets a detailed portrait and every character and enemy gets more detailed and more animated sprites. It's a relatively minor thing, but I loved the style of the first game and love it even more here.

Overall, the puzzles are a step up from the first game with some really genius solutions in places, and it's integrated with some neat lore based on a bunch of different mythologies like the first game (though mainly Norse here). Make sure you buy the TextTrax software and save any hints you can't figure out at the moment, but do be warned that right now there are a few mistranslations that get in the way, though I only recall one that prevented me from solving it without a walkthrough.

There have been some great improvements in movement and air control so it feels less like you're wrestling with some unforgiving controls and a couple weapons have been given some really nice rebalances. Everything just feels so much better to play than the first game. Which is good, because this game can be even more devious with the traps than the first game. Always be on the lookout for crushers in this game.

Speaking of weapons, you're gonna be taking on a lot of bosses and sub-bosses to progress. Not all of them are amazing, but there are some really interesting and fun fights in here. There were some that were either too hard or too easy in the initial release, but most of them have been rebalanced in patches since then. La-Mulana 2 is an amazing game and does a great job as a sequel to La-Mulana, but doesn't quite match its predecessor. It contains many allusions and spoilers for the first game, so make sure to play the earlier title first!

If you have played La-Mulana already I can wholeheartedly recommend buying this. It delivers on all the fronts the original did, gives you a whole new ruin to explore, complete with old and new characters and its own mythos to discover. 

If you have not played the previous game, don't hesitate and go play it first. I'm not writing this review for you.

[h1] Positives [/h1]
There have been a few improvements made compared to the first game.
[list]
[*]Lemeza moves around the screen a bit faster than her father and her young body allows her to keep some degree of control in the air after jumping. This is a nice quality-of-life change and makes it easier to navigate the ruins. 
[*]The location of tablets is more closely tied to the area where their hints are required. One common complaint in the first game was that tablets were often scattered around the ruins too much, making it hard to associate them with any puzzle. This has been fixed by placing the tablets more intelligently or by adding murals to the tablets that hint at the location they refer to, which also has the added benefit of looking pretty cool.
[*]Areas are more straight-forward to explore. There is an easily noticeable pattern among nearly all new areas of the ruins you can explore. 
[olist]
[*]The map is always found in one of the first rooms and unlockable by a relatively simple puzzle.
[*]The save point is also usually quite close to the entrance, reducing the amount of backtracking you have to do if you die.
[/olist]
This does not mean exploring the ruins is any easier or simpler.
[*]There are more NPCs that give you helpful hints if you're stuck, making some puzzles a little more transparent.
[*]The Glossary is a function of your in-game computer that contains information about all NPCs and enemies you encounter, and you can hunt for information on bosses too. It adds a lot of flavour to the game and can even help you figure out some puzzles.
[*]The world building, level design, room design, enemy design and the boss fights are amazing! Each area has its own history tied into the origins of the ruins and while they do feel a bit more samey this time around, the added story about the areas inhabitants and their relations towards each other, the ruins and the outside world more than makes up for it.
The areas feel cohesive and are littered with deadly traps more devious than in the first game. The enemies are creative, drawn from all kinds of mythologies and placed in a smart and annoying way, with equally annoying movement patterns, so as to require you to put some thought into maneuvering around them. 
Lastly, the boss fights are bombastic, unique and well designed, featuring amazing art and animations.
[*]Puzzle mechanics have been enhanced with a new layer. Many puzzles involve the chanting of mantras, which in my opinion made for some fun puzzles, which also leads me to my next point:
[*]There are no more trial-and-error mantra chases or anything similar! The game does a good job of giving you all the information you require. It is up to you to draw the correct conclusions.
[/list]

[h1]Shortcomings:[/h1]

[list]
[*]The in-game Text tracking methods are mostly the same as the last game and they are still not sufficient. You will have to keep notes somewhere else to advance through some puzzles without a major headache or getting stuck because you forgot a minor detail you were told earlier, but can't quite recall anymore. As I enjoy this kind of thing it wasn't a concern for me, but for those players who prefer to keep it in the game, a better way of storing the hints would have been highly desirable.
[*]The game doesn't tell you about the importance of NPCs. NPCs often give crucial hints or even unlock new paths if you visit them again after completing certain puzzles. This feels incredibly random and obtuse and was the cause of much frustration for me. Fortunately these instances weren't very frequent and once I knew to revisit the NPCs regularly I could adapt.
[*]The Unity Engine allows for some nice effects, but it causes slowdowns on older PCs. The game is still very playable and the slowdowns were not present during any boss fights for me. Still, for a game with La-Mulanas graphics I feel this should have been avoided.
[*]Everything is the same. Virtually every item you find in La-Mulana 2 has been in La-Mulana 1 already. The reasoning for this is explained in the story, and for many of the subweapons this makes sense mechanically. But I would have expected Nigoro to come up with more truly new items and mechanics regardless.
[*]The late game feels rushed. After some point in the game it felt like all that was left were boss rushes and no more puzzles to solve. I couldn't appreciate the many bosses because I got so tired of seeing them. The end game also is a glorified boss gauntlet and the final escape sequence was very lackluster with an obvious path compared to the first game. Still, by this point I had gotten so much enjoyment out of the game I was still glad to have completed it. Considering this, it says a lot that this is my biggest gripe with the game.
[*]There was one instance of a bad translation making it hard to solve a puzzle, but I expect this to be fixed soon, if it isn't already.
[/list]

[h1]Advice:[/h1]

To avoid any headaches or broken controllers during the game I recommend to follow these two guidelines:
[list]
[*]Keep notes on everything. Whether you use screenshots or write things down is up to you, but the in-game methods are only a supplement
[*]Regularly revisit NPCs as they will give you crucial hints for solving puzzles.
[/list]
If you follow this advice and enjoyed the La-Mulana remake there shouldn't be anything hindering your enjoyment of the game!

[h1]Conclusion (TL;DR):[/h1]

La-Mulana 2 delivers a new adventure for you to embark on with all the peaks and abysses you have come to know from the first installment. It improves on many (sadly not on all) of its old formulas and provides an experience that is probably impossible to find elsewhere. It improves on the previous game's world design and features neatly designed puzzles. Despite Nigoro claiming the game would be much shorter to complete compared to the remake, it took me 58 hours of in-game time and 73 hours of (Steam) real time with minor use of spoilers if I got truly stuck. I enjoyed every minute of it and it managed to captivate me for a good few feeks.

Had fun. I don't think there would ever be a world where this was better than the first game, but it does a decent job at iterating on what the first game does and at not totally embarrassing itself. If LM1R is a perfect score, this is... a B, maybe a B-? Which is still pretty decent.
If you walked away from LM1R (play it first btw) and thought "That was pretty good. I might want to experience something like that again." this will probably be worth your time.

I backed this game on day 1 on kickstarter 4 years ago after playing the first game, which was already one of my favorite games of all time.

La-Mulana 2 expands well on its predecessor, using references for nostalgia but also for puzzles (people who played the first game will have a little advantage but you can still solve it all with the info in the game) and improves on it (especially when it comes to movement, allowing you to move much more freely than before).

While there are references to La-Mulana 1, it never goes overboard; some subthemes such as [spoiler] the Dimensional Corridor's [/spoiler] are reused, also in the form of a few little notes in the areas soundtrack. 9/10.  Very solid.  Highly recommended.  But it's not as good as La-Mulana 1.  Let's look at it, shall we?

First thing you should know is that there is exactly one other game like La-Mulana (and the original freeware La-Mulana, but we're talking about the remake), and that game is La-Mulana 2.  So there's no alternative, really.  La-Mulana is a brutal puzzle-metroidvania, and until La-Mulana 2 came along, La-Mulana was the *only* brutal puzzle-metroidvania.  La-Mulana 2 features easily 100 hours of exploration and puzzle-solving.  My in-game completion time was over 106 hours, which is a lot.  I like to describe La-Mulana 1 as a cross between a puzzle hunt and a kick to the face.  La-Mulana 2 is somewhat less dependent on masochism, which is why 1 was better.

La-Mulana 1, the game, hates you, the player.  In contrast, Eg-Lana, the game world in LM2, hates Lumisa, your character.  (Without spoiling anything, this hatred is actually part of the plot.)  You will die repeatedly, with the justification that the ruins hate you.  But the puzzles aren't unfair.  None of them are.  The traps aren't unfair either; you usually get plenty of warning.  Usually.  Sometimes you don't, and it's funny to watch LPers fall to these traps.  The enemies will give you hell; there are a lot of them, and sometimes they get pretty overwhelming.  The bosses...  Mixed bag.  Some are very difficult; most are easily cheesed (though updates might have changed this since I beat them).  A lot of them are actually very memorable, but a lot are really not.  The final boss in particular is far easier than the final boss of LM1.  In LM1, I had a very hard time with the bosses; in LM2, not so much, and I don't think it's because I magically became that much of a better player.

The story in LM2 is quite detailed.  LM1 NPC's were mostly limited to random shops and random hints that could have been on tablets; LM2 features a broad array of actual characters, all with gorgeous art.  There's a significant retcon issue, because the stuff that happens in LM2 kind of shouldn't be possible given the setting of LM1, but eh, who really cares?  There is, however, a very heavy focus on Norse mythology, unlike in LM1.  LM1 had regions dedicated to different mythologies and decorated according to different cultures, but there's a much heavier focus on the intricacies of mythology here, especially Norse but also Japanese, Greek, a little Babylonian (less than LM1), Egyptian, etc.  There's a little bit of Mesoamerican, too; I don't think there are any Mesoamerican characters, but there are some minibosses and decorations from that set of mythologies.

In terms of gameplay, Lumisa controls kind of quirkily.  She's more fluid than Lemeza in LM1, but you'll find yourself relying on timing and careful jumps to hit bosses, and if you don't know what you're doing, you'll just die quickly.  Luckily, the platforming isn't so bad.  Some very late-game challenges and bosses stretch your ability to use Lumisa's movement, but you get movement upgrades that make things a lot nicer, especially in the realm of weapons.  Many people are immediately turned off by the lack of fluidity, which is actually used in puzzle-solving.  I personally don't think that this lack of fluidity is a problem at all.

LM2 is more of a metroidvania than LM1, and that's a pretty great thing, in my opinion.  There are many helpful upgrades and collectibles.  LM1 had a lot of one-time-use items or passive items that unlocked one thing.  LM2 has some of those, sure, but it also has a lot of items that are more general-purpose.  That kind of thing just feels good to play.  Not that La-Mulana 2 should be trying to make anyone feel good, but hey.

On the other hand, this game has a lot of handholding when it comes to the mechanics.  Some basic puzzles involving movement are actually spelled out for you, unlike in LM1.  In the first game, there was very little guidance; you'd get some vaguely cryptic hints from Xelpud and everything else was trial and error.  LM2 actually spells it out for you.  I think that this is one point where LM1 is stronger, but the problem is that LM2 is aimed at people who have played LM1 and therefore already know those mechanics, so it makes sense to explain them.  You should feel lost when you first start to play LM1, but if you play LM1, you won't feel lost when playing LM2.  The handholding is fair to new players, I'd say.

On my 6-year-old Mac, LM2 ran... OK.  Some rooms and bosses consistently slowed down.  I watched some LP's and they did not get the slowdowns, so it might be just me or just the Mac or something, I don't know.  Some people really care about this sort of thing.  I don't.

Now, the main event: the puzzles!  I won't spoil anything, but I will say that LM2 is DENSE with puzzles.  There are a whole lot of them -- 106 hours' worth, for me!  And here's the best part: if you're conscientious about it, it can all be done without a guide.  I have to say that I used a guide for one thing, one time: at the 102 hour mark, I was looking for a particular optional item just to complete my inventory (it was not necessary to beat the game), and I used a guide to find out where it was after diligently checking every corner (it turns out that the tool I was using to check didn't work for this particular secret).  Other than that, though, the puzzles are very fair and very solvable, so long as you have persistence and don't miss hints!  Compared to LM1, there are a lot more puzzles, but for the most part they're less expansive.  There were many multi-step puzzles in LM1; in LM2, there are much fewer, and instead, there are a lot of single-room puzzle set-pieces.  On the other hand, there are a few big puzzles in LM2, and these are some of the most interesting puzzles in videogaming.  Some puzzles in LM1 were really quite unfair; LM2 tones the unfairness way down while maintaining most of the difficulty.  There are a few major bottlenecks where a necessary puzzle is not well-signposted, but that's kind of par for the course.  A few of them got me stuck for hours.  One in particular involves a one-time permanent change in a room; if you miss the animation the first time, you won't know that it changed.  That said, I did figure them out eventually!  Running around not knowing how to progress is one of the great points of this game.

As a final note, LM1 is completely groundbreaking.  When you play it, you've never seen anything like it; it has a huge wow factor.  LM2 doesn't, for pretty obvious reasons, so it unfortunately suffers from a kind of sequelitis, where it simply can't attain the purity of gameplay of the original because the original has already been done.  LM2 therefore doesn't surpass LM1 overall, despite its many improvements to the formula.  But from LM1, it's a LONG way down.  LM2 may not be the absolute best game ever made -- that's LM1 -- but it's right up there.

PS: DON'T USE A GUIDE.  THE FRUSTRATION IS PART OF THE FUN.  DON'T DO IT!

Having backed La-Mulana 2 on Kickstarter (for the pre-Brexit Sterling equivalent of $45) many years ago now I'd be remiss to not write at least something about it considering I've waited long enough for it. It's overall been a great experience, and I've definitely gotten my money's worth, but here're a few of my more pressing thoughts I wanted to share: 

La-Mulana games set their stalls out as being difficult, and as I noted in my review of the original, one of the great joys about exploring the ruins of La-Mulana was their complete indifference to life. You were thrown in with no idea of what was going on, nor what you were getting into, and frankly the game didn't give a toss whether you lived or died. You were fighting against a plausibly real place. Eg-Lana, for better or worse, has been designed by a far more malevolent hand; instant-death traps will give you no hint of their presence, spikes are laid not only as traps but as damage-dealers looking nothing more than to collect a knockback and, even without hard mode, the game's enemy count scales with how many of a certain necessary item you collect. Even at full health, a single hit can cause a knockback cascade that has you out on your arse in seconds. This place isn't indifferent to you: it actively hates you, and while not being a complaint about difficulty this does make the experience far less organic and more "gamey". I was clearly trying to beat a designer here, not a ruin, and I occasionally found that immersion-breaking.

This is a pity because the environments themselves are a real delight: although the first few fields are clearly grounded in Norse mythology they soon give way to impressively-styled Egyptian, Greek, Japanese and Indian-themed fields, and a few surprises that I wasn't expecting, all accompanied by equally superb soundtracks. I was somewhat sceptical of their choice of Unity for the engine when it was first announced but it doesn't take too much in-game time to see why it was the right decision. Having that 3rd dimension to play with means the lighting is consistently a cut above anything the first game had to offer, and the few 3d elements that are used on the stages themselves serve to make the place feel "solid" to great effect.

I can't go any further into this without talking about the boss fights (which I know have been patched since I beat it) but I'm going to come straight out with it - they're the worst part of the game. That's certainly not for want of imagination: the bosses and battlegrounds themselves look good and are varied enough, and the musical score will definitely get you pumped up and ready for a fight, but the fight designs themselves are just... Uninspired. Once you've got your attack strategy figured out you'll just go through the motions until either the boss dies, or you do. Every boss having multiple phases with much wider variance in attack would have helped mitigate this tremendously, but by the time this happens it's too little, too late.

Where La-Mulana 2 really shines are the puzzles. For the most part it's items from the first game making a re-appearance, but the order you get them in leaves far more scope for problem solving, a scope La-Mulana 2 meets and then some. Literally every tablet serves a purpose (even if you don't know what it is), and writing things down goes from desirable to utterly essential. The addition of the race scanner is genius and solves at a stroke one of the bigger issues with the first game; namely the lack of connection between the location of a clue and the location you apply it in. The game does a fantastic job of making you feel clever, and "Aha!" moments abound. "These puzzles make no sense!" was, if my own see-hearing was anything to go by, the #1 complaint about La-Mulana 1. Trust me, with the exception of a single translation issue (that is known, and being fixed), this game atones for that entirely.

So there we have it; some thoughts on La-Mulana 2 (I told you they were condensed!). Rarely poor, often excellent, sometimes incredible, and that's probably the most upsetting thing of all because in my opinion this is, overall, an excellent sequel doomed to live in the shadow of an original that for me is still one of the greatest games ever made. La-Mulana 2 does so much right; the depth, the environments, the music, the puzzles, the uncompromising difficulty, that if you've got any love for indie platforming I can't not recommend it. It's just a damned shame that the first did all of that right as well, and in years to come, that'll be the one that gets remembered.

La-Mulana 2 has a few new features. First, NPCs now have names and faces, and most of the NPCs living inside the ruins are gods and other mythological figures. NOTE: I made it roughly halfway before hitting another progress bottleneck that lasted [i]12 hours[/i] before I gave up and started using a guide for the rest of the way. This review may or may not reflect that

So, La Mulana 2. Heard about it many years ago, and honestly forgot about it after a while, figuring it must have gone the route of so many other kickstarters until suddenly, it shows up on my store page. I liked La-Mulana and played it a decade ago and honestly, this review is going to be almost entirely applicable to the first game as well.

The first thing you need to know about this game is this isn't your average metroidvania, and I would not recommend this full stop to anyone who merely likes the genre. This game has a hard as nails puzzle element to it and gives the old Sierra games and their knockoffs a run for their money for amount of time you'll spend frustratedly scratching your head trying to figure out what the hell to do next. This is what I call a "progress bottleneck". Where your range of things you can do narrows down to just a few or even one possibility, in this case among 300+ or so rooms. Little needle, big haystack.

I, personally, didn't watch enough Rick and Morty and thus stumbled across the first half of the game hitting progress bottleneck after progress bottleneck for hours each until I finally reached the point where in two days using all of my free time - 12 hours - I had made absolutely no progress whatsoever, having read every tablet several times, and even gone mad and spent a ridiculous amount of money on subweapons to strike at damn near every damn pixel of the game for secret god damn walls. I didn't want hundreds of hours of my life to end up being consumed trying to solve these agonizing progress bottlenecks, so I elected to admit I'm a dummy, swallow my pride, and use guides for much of the remainder. Keep in mind that if you want to beat this game without using guides or cheating, you will have to be very smart at this sort of thing and have a lot of patience. I don't really hold this against this game, it's just that this degree and type of challenge isn't really my cup of tea. If it's yours, [i]then you should absolutely buy this game and play it right now, you absolute madman.[/i]

So the puzzles are hard, good that I spent a long winding/whining paragraph to let you know that "the puzzles are hard". The point I'm trying to get across is this isn't Cave Story, this isn't SotN, this isn't Rabi-Ribi, it's a vastly different experience than any of those, which means on one hand that you shouldn't listen to anyone who tells you "if you like metroidvanias, you'll love this!" and at the same time if metroidvanias aren't usually your cup of tea but mindfucking puzzles are, this might be the metroidvania for you. 

As for the rest of the game? Let's just say this would be one of my favorites if it were made more accessible to idiots like me. Combat is usually pretty fluid yet simple and clunky, but I have a hard time saying it's clunky in a bad way. weapons have absolute areas of damage that can feel unweildy but if you get the hang of it, can be very useful, such as the whip with it striking slightly above and behind you before striking ahead. There's a good variety of sub-weapons(basically ammo-consuming weapons) that cover much of your needs. Bosses are usually fun to play against, having that satisfying sequence of learning the pattern while you die a dozen times before getting the hang of it and ruining their shit, which is my kind of bosses.

However, I have two gripes about combat. One, a lot of bosses are picky as hell about what registers as a hit, one of the earliest examples being nidhogg. There's often not any real indicator to what you have to hit and often it's a small window that doesn't make logical sense. There's only a few cases where this gets controller-chucking annoying, though. There's also the problem that while the game gives you controls to cycle through weapons/subweapons, you don't get the option to control what order, or which to cycle through at any given time. This can get frustrating when your strategy involves two subweapons nearly equally far apart on your cycle, and often forces you to switch through the game's menu or else risk costly failures.

Finally, the graphics of this game are just fantastic. Especially the environmental art. The music is pretty good but I still miss the classic style tunes of OG La-Mulana and would kill for such versions of this game's music. The story was pretty engaging, but one little nitpick I have is that characters have less and less to say to you as the game progresses, the last quarter of the game until the very end being almost completely devoid of any interaction with the rest of the main cast, through visiting them or receiving messages.

Overall, If you loved the original La-Mulana, I really don't think this game will fail to live up to your expectations and you should just get it. Otherwise, it's kind of hard to really pin what I want to say in conclusion here. This game is pretty niche, and that's not something anyone should hold against it. I gave up but got the sense that it does what it does very well. I recommend this game specifically for the kind of niche it fills. If you love ridiculously challenging puzzles of this sort, this is for you. If you dislike it, I can't say you're gonna like this game.

The original La-Mulana is one of my favorite games of all time and in my opinion damn near close to a perfect game. The remake of La-Mulana improved the game in a lot of areas mainly making the action part of the game much better but it scaled back on the puzzles which was my favorite part of the original and thus I didn't like it as much though it was still a good game. Following the same pattern as the remake the puzzles in this game were scaled back while the action parts of the game were scaled up. The problem is La-Mulana was never about it's action elements for me but the puzzles and it's honestly a shame.

That's not to say all the puzzles are brainless. A lot of the early ones are but later in the game they get a bit creative and I like a lot of them. The Mantra puzzles are all kinda bad mostly cause the game highlights the mantras essentially telling you flat out use x mantra in x room. When the puzzles are good though they're good. I can't help but feel the puzzles are also less elegantly implemented as one thing I liked about the original was most of the puzzles were based in the games lore while the puzzles in this game feel almost just attached on to their already created areas. This may also be a fault of the translation as I've noticed several gramatical errors and name errors throughout the game which tells me the translation isn't of the highest quality.

While the combat engine is much better in this game but I can't help but feel like the combat is just worse than the original. While there are some pretty cool bosses in this game there are also some really really bad bosses. The final boss itself was also kinda a let down. The game features a lot more subbosses but they are pretty easily cheesable by braking there AI. Overall while the combat engine is better I don't feel like they really used it to it's full potential.

The map layout I find to be worse than the original as well. There are several areas in the game that just aren't very memorable while in the original every area felt like they all tied together. Anothe issue I have with the map layout is that the game kinda forces you on a linear path for a while. You pretty much have to beat the first boss to get anywhere and then you have to beat the next 2 to really open up the game. After that your back to your whole metroidvania experience but the long tutorialish section of the game didn't really appeal to me. In the original you had 4 areas you could explore right from the getgo but here you can only really access one extra area before fighting the first boss and you can't really even do much there..

The Graphics in the game where really well done. I like all the character portrait designs you see throughout the game. The music was good and there are some killer tracks though I think overall it was a step down from the first games. Though it is kinda hard to beat the originals tracks so I can't blame them too much for not succeeding here.

Another issue with this game that will hopefully be fixed is that it's really buggy right now. It's not unplayable but you'll run into a bug or two throughout your game that will likely cause you to reset. Also changing your controls doesn't change menu controls which really blows.

Overall while I have ragged on the game a lot that's mostly cause I've been comparing it to the original games which as I stated were damn near perfect. While I think the game failed to capture what made La-Mulana so great it's still a great game that is definitely worth your time. Just don't expect too much or you'll be disappointed.

Consider Pascal’s Wager. Even with the slightest chance that God exists, only a fool would bet against his existence, given that the stakes are so high. But what happens if you’ve worshipped in the wrong deity all along? Among those gods from Greek, Egyptian, Mesopotamian mythologies, they can’t all have presence over the world, right? Or can they? What if the gods are driven by a even greater force? Well, welcome to Mulana and Eg-Lana.

La-Mulana 2 is an extremely open-ended Metroidvania that blends archeology with mythology. Similar to an amalgamation of carrot juice and apple juice, it tastes unsmooth at first, but once I’ve got into it, I just couldn’t resist. Sleep begins to elude me. 

Guacamelee informs that you can’t break a red block until you’ve acquired the uppercut ability, and lots of modern Metroidvania titles have their emphasis on abilities and gear. La-Mulana 2 is eccentric in this sense, as it barely sets a clear barrier in your way at any time. By obtaining double jump, you’d expect that it opens the world with tons of fresh new opportunities, but it doesn’t, as much. In fact, such movement enhancement is more useful traversing rooms than unlocking items and reaching new areas. 

In my own words, La-Mulana 2 is a lore-based Metroidvania, making progress isn’t as simple as obtaining a certain skill to break a certain block. The player is expected to learn about the ruin, gather scattered information, solve cryptic yet not overly obscure puzzles, and ultimately, unravel the secrets of Eg-Lana. The most useful upgrades in the game aren’t those that help you bypass obstacles, but rather those which assist you in traversing rooms to collect information, that is, health orbs, double jump, weapon upgrades, etc. You’ll eventually need the former upgrades, but only after solving the puzzles at first.

“Hardcore” is an overly used term nowadays, as most gamers and developers view it as a tag rather than a definition. And I’ve seen desperate attempts aiming to resemble such “hardcoreness” and fail, as those developers mistook “trial and error” for “hardcore”. Sometimes “hardcore” and “user experience” collide with each other, games with comprehensive tutorials are spoon-feeding knowledge to gamers, which isn’t necessary a bad thing, but it does rob the fun of players discovering game mechanics on themselves. Celeste only taught the players a few advanced tricks near the end of the game, leaving a variety of movesets yet to be uncovered. La-Mulana 2 went a lot further, leaving almost everything to the player’s imagination and inspection. Imagine Lumiza attending a training session learning how to whip, leap and place weights in the village before departing to the ruins, why would a well-trained archeologist do such thing?

La-Mulana 2 is a “seek and you shall find” kind of game, which expects the player to learn and develop their style of play through indirect assistance. Such design, as with fireworks, should be tread with extra care. I assume the developers learnt from criticisms of the first game, and added a pre-game area in which serves as an “open-world tutorial”, the Mulana ruins. The player wanders around, learns about the plot from the original game and get used to the flow of the moveset while obtaining essential starting items. Additionally, when you make it to Roots of Yggdrasil, the first area in Eg-Lana where the real game takes place, your exploration is pretty limited until you’ve solved the puzzle of the three goddesses and defeated Farnir, the one of many guardians. With that being said, the Mulana ruins and Roots of Yggdrasil serve as the basic tutorial and puzzle tutorial respectively. Upon defeating Farnir, you’ll start to feel the scope and depth of such open-ended Metroidvania. But fear nothing for the world is boundless, as each humble step counts toward the whole.

I do think there’re two puzzles that leap way out of bound in terms of logic, namely the usage of the pepper, and the riddle of the colossal dragon tangling with the infernal beast. Oh well, maybe it’s because the scripts weren’t properly translated into Chinese. As for the other puzzles, with the scope ranging from a single room to places scattered across multiple areas, are fair and reasonable, some of which are exceedingly well designed. 

The seven gates of eternal prison puzzle is a noteworthy one. I’m supposed to enter seven gates in a certain order to unlock a seal, and passing through each gate disables one of my items. Hints about this puzzle trace back to early tablets in Divine Fortress, which I’ve scanned during my first 5 hours in the game. You may be confused, isn’t this a terrible terrible design which forces you to revisit old places aimlessly until you’ve found the information that you’ve overlooked? The fact is, the puzzle can be solved without any additional hints, that only “pass seven gates” and “each gate robs you an item” are sufficient for solving the puzzle. Each gate robs you an item, thus limits your mobility and rules out the possibility of reaching certain gates. By creating a checklist of which gate should be passed before when, you’ll be able to determine the correct order of the gates without additional assistance. It’s true that this puzzle would be much easier with the help of the tablets in Divine Fortress, as you’ll get the full ordering by solving an easy semiotic puzzle, but what fascinates me is the flexibility in solving this. Maybe you’ve lost track of one or two relevant tablets, and still been able to solve it through logic reasoning filling up the gaps.

I’m not a big fan of the platforming and the controls. You lose 90% control of Lumisa when she gets hit in the air. Along with no invincibility frame to spikes, this may easily result in you being juggled around several times, having a majority of your health drained. Also, teleport tablets don’t heal you, which is absurd given that you can simply teleport to the village then teleport back when fully healed. However, I do respect the developers for making these decisions, maybe they thought such feature gives the game its hardcore credentials.

Right now I’m motivated to play the original game, given that the sequel is so good. I might be disappointed, as La-Mulana 2 has clearly improved through taking into account all the criticisms of La-Mulana. The question is, exactly by how much? Am I really into this genre? We shall see.

+Improved graphics are great.

One of my favorite flawed series. The La-Mulana games are 2D metroidvanias with a lot of emphasis on exploration and puzzle solving. You will gain only a few mobility upgrades, but will gain a lot of artifacts needed to solve puzzle.

It is not a game for everyone. The puzzles are confusing, and the combat is tough and can be janky at times. But it's also overall a far better experience than the first episode (if that's where you are coming from). 

You will still need to take a lot of notes, maybe make your own maps to remember places of interest, and pay attention to clues, as they range from hints to the current or nearby puzzle room, to cosmic brain meta bread crumbs for late game stuff.

If you choose to try your chance, you will be looking at some really nice pixel art, and will listen to great tunes along the way. You are also looking to around 40+ hours of playtime (double that if you are adamant on not using a guide).

I'd suggest you try your best to not use a guide as long as you can. And even if you do, try not to rely on it too much and solve stuff on your own instead, as I believe it will make the experience more gratifying. No judgment though, I did use a guide at some point every playthrough I went through.

A few hints (no spoilers): 
- The game is an open ended metroidvania, and you can push really far into the game while having skipped some important upgrade, or missed some vital clues, so if you are stuck on a puzzle, the answer might be somewhere else entirely. 
- While back tracking inside Eg-Lana is the name of the game, try to revist places outside of Eg-Lana regularly. 
- Talk and re talk to NPC often. 
- Read the tablet texts, but look at the pictures if there is one, as they are often great clues themselves
- Look at the background too!
- Never assume that a new area is not explorable in your current state. You will probably find more clues there!
- Don't be afraid to fight sub bosses, they often guard new areas or items and generally only have a few patterns to learn.

Incredibly Frustrating But a Unique Gaming Experience

The La Mulana series is all about exploring a vast and opaque complex of ruins with dense lore and deep mysteries. I keep coming back to La Mulana because very few exploration/adventure/metroidvania games give you a very real sense of discovery. You will feel like a total badass as you slowly work your way through these ruins solving puzzles and pushing your skills - you're basically thrown into the deep end and expected to swim and it feels like a real accomplishment when you figure things out on your own. 

The major problem with this game and its predecessor is that the last third of the game - the really deep and involved puzzles - can be nearly impossible to figure out on your own. They involve remembering clues from 100 rooms ago and combining that with 5 other clues all equally obscure, or needing to break a particular wall with little to no clue which one it is... gets very frustrating and sometimes feels like you needed to be able to read the developer's minds to understand the solution. There's a very robust community of guides, maps, and walkthroughs because they are nearly essential to complete the game (some hardcore people might insist on doing it alone, but after 20 hours of wandering around rereading clues it's more fun to just look it up online). To really get the most out of the game be prepared to take screenshots of every tablet, make your own maps on paper, etc. 

Despite all of that, and no matter how much this game had me cursing it, overall it delivers a really unique experience that games don't really deliver anymore. The game play elements are dense (lots of items to use and equip, skills that can combo,, etc.), the progression is really well though out in terms of finding a new clue that leads down a rabbit hole to the next clue or item, and you end up really feeling like a badass Indiana Jones. 

Get the game, push yourself as far as you absolutely can. Push yourself a little more. When you're finally ready to give up check a guide, and go a little further.

I have taken my time with La-Mulana 2 and seeing as how it’s been out for a month, this review might be too late.  I wanted to be sure to explore all aspects of the game and give the best insights I could.  With a game like this, it’s impossible to give anything other than first impressions even after 20-30 hours.

La-Mulana 2 has been in development for 4-5 years and I backed it on kickstarter after enjoying the hell out of the first one.  After playing, I can say that if you enjoyed the first, you will most definitely enjoy this one but that isn’t to say it doesn’t have its fair share of criticisms.

La-Mulana 2 follows Lumisa Kosugi as she explores the ancient ruins of La-Mulana. Desperate to find the cause of the recent slew of monsters appearing from the ruins, Lumisa discovers the "other" La-Mulana: the ruins known as Eg-Lana.
It’s a metroidvania with a high focus on puzzle solving and tight platforming over action.

I would like to get the bad things out of the way first, because while this game is to be praised, it is not flawless.  For those who do not know what La-Mulana is, it’s a side scrolling puzzle game akin to difficulty from the old NES era video games.  Players will have to take physical notes, screenshots, and pay attention to virtually every detail in each room in order to successfully complete this game with no hints.

However, many puzzles simply require better hints.  I tried to play this game with zero help and upon release, brought out my pen and paper to begin taking as many furious notes as I could.  Where the very map shape can be the solution to a puzzle, I cannot stress how important it is to write down names of the room and decorations.  While this game has a more linear fashion than the first, this doesn’t mean you cannot forge your own path.  It’s beyond frustrating to retract your steps for 4-5 hours to finally give in and notice that the progress forward was some obscure hint that you would have never considered.  This isn’t to say the puzzles are bad, in fact they are better than the first, but there were a few times that I was just stumped, even after seeing the solution.

Bosses are fantastic and gigantic.  The only real challenge from them, after beating them the first time, is to try them in hard mode with no sub weapons.  Many can simply be glitched and cheesed with a few sub weapons or by manipulating the AI.  They are not nearly as awesome as the first set, and I was sad to say that the last boss was recycled from the first one with a few extra phases.  Some were thought to be simply unbeatable, Kujata in patch 1.2.2.2 was beyond difficult to the average user and without some serious grinding, was no doubted where people stopped on their hard mode play through.  Thankfully the dev team is on top of things and they fixed it within a few days.  There are many who will say that boss designs are bad but I disagree and think that while many need polish, they’re unique and fun, albeit frustrating while you figure them out.

The music is just as gorgeous with so many memorable tracks.  Each boss has their own theme and the mood fits well.  This is by far my favorite aspect of the game and was my favorite of the first.  Graphics are definitely a step up from the first and runs on unity with many 3D elements in the background to give more depth.  The lore allows us to go deeper than the first as we learn about previous races and even go to space to see the first visitors to the planet!

I would absolutely recommend this game but only if you are a masochist.  I will fully admit this game is infuriating and frustrating to the point of breaking a controller, but when you spend hours trying to find a solution and FINALLY solve it, the rush of endorphins causes you to press on.

[b]tl;dr[/b] - A very specific kind of game for a very specific kind of person. If you're into obtuse puzzles that require excessive note taking and still lead you aimlessly wandering around, this is a wonderful game. As long as you're also fine with a relatively challenging 2D platformer on top of that. And La-Mulana 2 is broadly an upgrade to La-Mulana, so if you liked the original, or were close to liking it, you can view this as an improvement.

Much like the original La-Mulana, La-Mulana 2 is a great game that's very easy to hate. To some degree, the game is a challenge mechanically. Normal enemies can often be deadly, navigating a few screens can kill you, bosses might take dozens of attempts, and you'll have to preapre to repeatedly fail jumps. But at the end of the day, if you like 2D platformers you'll probably be able to handle almost all of that. La-Mulana 2 is also drastically more forgiving than La-Mulana was in these regards, the ability to control yourself mid-jump alone is a godsend compared to the very locked-in movement of La-Mulana.

However there's two things that could entirely turn you off the game. The first are the games many, many puzzles. The first chest in the game requires a puzzle (albeit one with an obvious explanation handed to you to get the ball rolling). Everything you do after that will be based on puzzles as well. You will likely require a pencil and paper to play this game. If you summarize only important information you're likely to miss clues and be left wondering what to do for hours. If you write down everything you'll accrue dozens of pages before you're halfway through the game. And you're still likely to get lost wondering what to do for hours anyway.

This is made worse by the game's almost complete lack of quality-of-life features. You have to find the maps for each area, even though they're usually the first chest you'll see upon arriving. Those maps don't keep track of even basic things like the entrances to the areas without upgrading, and will never keep track of even something as simple as which rooms you have and haven't visited or how they link together. There's an in-game note taking tool that can easily be filled in the first few areas if you use it too judiciously. To even read any of the tablets required to solve puzzles requires buying an item in the opening town which is only explained to you in the game's manual, accessable from the website.

These two are very interlinked. It's easy to miss things when it's hard to keep track of what you've done, and it's hard to keep track of everything you need to do when the game provides no tools to help you. That said, if you have a solid memory or a lot of patience, and feel like you've got some solid problem solving tools under your belt (and enjoy 2D platformers) this game can be a lot of fun. There are few experiences as rewarding as solving a challenging puzzle on your own or coming back to do something you found impossible before (whether because you couldn't figure it out or it was too mechanically challenging).

So I recommend La-Mulana 2, to a very specific kind of person. And if you get easily angry, or easily bored, or don't want to keep your own notes, or don't like challening gameplay, or don't like obtuse puzzles, this game isn't for you. But to that other kind of person, La-Mulana 2 fills a niche that few other games do, and does so better than almost any of them. It's the kind of experience you can't get anywhere else, and that makes it well worth the money if it's the kind of game you'd want to play.

And if you were so-so on La-Mulana and are wondering if La-Mulana 2 is worth picking up, I'd say it's a large improvement in many ways. Like being able to control yourself in the air, as mentioned. The puzzles are generally less obtuse and the game requires less going back and forth between areas repeatedly while making very little progress. I've found the bosses to be more fun (generally). Maybe most importantly, there are almost no ways to permanently lock yourself out of things in La-Mulana 2 as compared to La-Mulana.

A final note, as of this writing the game does have a small number of bugs. Nothing game breaking any longer, I don't think, but it is something to be aware of. Given the pace they've been being fixed at, and the stability of La-Mulana at this point, I have full confidence they won't be along for that much longer.

If you aren't familiar with this series, it is an action-platformer with puzzle/exploration elements for progression. You can run, jump, and whip things like a Castlevania game, but you can also scan tablets and areas for cryptic in-universe clues that lead you towards solving puzzles, such as using certain items in specific areas. These can reveal traps, hidden passages, or treasures. The game is divided into approximately 14 or so major areas, with 9 or 10 bosses, and over 40 sub bosses with specific lore and attack patterns.

The controls will take getting used to. It uses arrows and Z/X for jumping and attacks, plus C/V for additional items. These can all be rebound, and playing on a controller is recommended (but not required). Soundtrack seems like it has fewer memorable tracks compared to the first game, but the two or three that I liked were really, [i]really[/i] good.

For veterans of the first game, it's exactly what you want from a sequel: more of the same, but done better. Movement is more fluid, the routing is less linear, puzzle difficulty is around the same (though I didn't have to resort to a guide this time around, since I knew what to expect). Without any spoilers, there are a few bosses that are spiritual successors to previously clunkier bosses in the first game, and it was amazing to see how they reused the concept but done "right".

It is however, a new release and the developers burned out a bit towards the end (and it shows), but there has been a post-release effort to polish it, just as the first game was. So.

Overall, I would [u]strongly recommend[/u] this game if you enjoy Metroidvania games. The controls and general difficult (both against bosses and wasting 30h+ running around trying to remember where you saw that damn tablet that had a relevant hint) might be a turn-off to some people, but it is very fun and worth the money.

Overall the game is a worthy companion to La-Mulana Remake. Nigoro had the seemingly insurmountable task of following up their magnum opus. While I can't say La-Mulana 2 is a superior game, it definitely provides more of what the first game offered: puzzles that span multiple rooms over spans of game progression, unique platforming and combat, iconic art design, and orgasmic soundtrack.

This game is HARD, I think to a detriment where the final 1/3 of the game is overwhelming with what the player is expected to remember on top of extreme platformer difficulty. Nigoro incorporated a dynamic difficulty where the collection of crystal skulls spawned more enemies in the stages, as a way to keep the game paced to the player's progress. They overshot this, because after the 6th skull, the game essentially becomes the Hard Mode. Advancing through the Underworld is quite possibly the most involved puzzle experience I had in a video game, so much I may as well have been attempting the real thing like Odysseus (the Underworld even has Eurydice!). Honestly I could not get past the Underworld, it's too difficult. However, it is quite thrilling and intense. I'm positive that anyone who overcame the Underworld, defeating its boss, would agree that the Underworld left them exhausted but fulfilled.

The assets are splendid. Lemeza is more animated than her father. Kabandha should be the game's mascot. Mythology is much more woven to the gameplay. Although there are more stages in total than its predecessor, the stages stand out and feel complete. Infact, where the first game did have fields that felt too similar, Nigoro made sure that the sequel's fields each stands on its own. Navigation, especially the shortcuts like Corridor of Blood, illustrate the labyrinthine complexity of Eg-Lana.

The music is a slower-boil approach. The first game needed to meet MSX standards in its original, so each of its songs need to snap-captivate the player. Thus it's easy to recollect a La-Mulana song because the first 20 seconds sets up everything about the given field's composition. Here with La-Mulana 2, each song is a longer affair, where the content is immediately obvious in the first 30 seconds. So my initial impression not feeling impressed by the soundtrack. However the longer I played, the more I realized my attachment to the later points of a given song, even 2 minutes into it.

In case you haven't played the first game, a warning is in place: this game, like the first one, is only beatable without external help by a person with incredible patience, attention to detail and capacity for drawing connections between disjointed information. This game resembles research work, dealing with a large amount of clues and making educated guesses on where the next weak spot for progress is. It should be noted that mandatory items may be hidden behind innocuous looking breakable walls and other dastardly secrets, although in practically every case there is in hindsight some reason to suspect that specific place. Still, the posibility of being stuck later on cause you didn't test whipping one wall in a suspicious place is very much real.

Also, even outside puzzles, expect the game to have a sense of humor that is not afraid to joke with the player's life. Spikes and other hazards seem like they're placed by a master troll, and instant deathtraps of various degrees of unexpectedness are not uncommon. Thankfully getting unexpectedly squished or the like is typically a very small loss of progress, and at least to me feels like a joke and an extra bit of information.

The upsides are an immense, absorbing game with a great soudtrack, fascinating backstory, great varied locales, decently good boss fights, an interesting sense of humor, and a real sense of investigating a complex ruin. It's definitely not a game for everyone, but for the ones who are receptive to it, it's a one-of-a-kind experience.

Now, compared to the first La-Mulana:
- The sequel is about as enormous as the first game, possibly even slightly larger.
- The sequel's backstory and overall storytelling is much more involved and expanded.
- The sequel does a better job of teaching new players at the start before it opens up and linearity goes off the window.
- The sequel's soudtrack is about on par with the original's, except maybe suffering a bit in boss music.
- Speaking of bosses, the sequel unfortunately seems to be a bit more hit and miss in this area, compared to the consistent quality of the first game.

The release has had some nasty bugs, but seemingly the worst of them have been eliminated so far. Still some lingering about, though. It also should be noted that there are a lot of major spoilers for the first La Mulana, even very early on in the game.

The sequel to La Mulana, a game that attempted to emulate a non-existent era of pathetically bad controls married to excellent presentation, mildly improves the controls but still leaves you randomly wandering a bunch of pointlessly convoluted corridors with platformer controls that were done better as early as the original Super Mario, if not before.

This is compounded by a world with sparse save points and instakill traps, because what I love more than anything is after spending half an hour trying to figure out what the developer was smoking during the design of a specific section, then having to redo it all again because a platform that looked a pixel off from another platform would instantly kill me.

Even when you're doing things right, it feels like you're exploiting edge cases in the game's atrocious air control and jumping(yes, bad jumping and air control, in a PLATFORMER) to accomplish anything at all, and extremely basic navigation options like "jumping off ladders" are gated behind ability progression later in the game.

La Mulana 1 and 2 are both excellent examples of everything that's wrong with retro gaming: mistaking technological design limitations and early game design mistakes, for wonderful concepts that should be replicated and carried into the future. Like I get it, you were traumatized by some bad games when you were a kid, but that doesn't mean you need to hurt others. You can let the trauma die and just make a good game instead.

Mind you, I wouldn't be half as upset by the game being as bad as it is if it wasn't presented wonderfully. So maybe just turn it on and have the soundtrack running in the background while you play a better platformer. Lord knows it isn't a challenge to find one.

There is a stark contrast between this game and its predecessor. Whereas exploring the original La Mulana was a treat, embarking on new journeys and discovering interesting lore, the sequel feels painful. I had a hard time getting started in game, since the tutorial barely tells you anything. And keep in mind, I have played and beaten the previous game! It's just not intuitive, and the character handling is odd in the best of situations. There are hidden gems in the game everywhere, but you really do have to spend a ridiculous amount of time looking for them.

The game definitely got better graphics from the original, but that's about it. It's just a confusing mess.

Game is purposedly engineered to make you waste as much time as possible.
- Controlling the character for simple things like jumping is made very difficult.
- Traps that kill in one hit, making you restart at your last save and lose progress.
- Only one save place per area.
- Health restoration is only available by teleporting back to the start of the game.
- Obtuse puzzles with obscure hints that have you wandering around aimlessly for hours.
- Simplistic bosses that are only hard because they hit you for too much damage. If you thought silksong was bad this is worse.

All in all a very poor excuse for a game.

La-Mulana 2 is a game that is a less of a sequel to the original and more the original: part 2. That is to say, it's a game that's very much the same as the original, not introducing any new flaws or drastic changes, but also doing nothing to iron out the problems the original had.
I only got 2 because I heard that the puzzles were significantly less obtuse this time around, and quite frankly, that was complete bull. The puzzles in 2 are every bit as obtuse and esoteric as in the first game, and while it feels great when you're making progress and exploring new areas, getting stuck combing over the entire available game world trying to find any hint that will get you to somewhere or something new is what will occupy the bulk of any first playthrough. This is on top of LM2 having an abundance of cheap instant kill traps, far more than I remember the first game having, and with even less indication of those traps being present this time around, if at all. So in some ways 2 has actually taken steps backwards by being more trial and error focused so it can say "haha I got you!", with one great example being a room with a miniboss and a trap designed to evoke memories of a similar boss in the first game, but if you try to evade the trap in the same way you'll be killed right away. That said, all the minibosses and ankh bosses are significantly easier this time around, so you'll be dying far more to traps than anything else in 2.

If you liked the first game then La Mulana 2 will satisfy your desire for more of it. If you sort of liked the first game but wished it wasn't as obnoxiously vague with its puzzles then 2 will do nothing to appeal to you more. For me, the enjoyment of exploring new areas and solving puzzles loses to the frustration of spending hours not getting anywhere at all and losing progress to invisible instant death traps.

I didn't like the first La Mulana game, but I liked certain aspects of it. I heard this game was much better about the misdirection and long drawn out puzzles. While that's entirely true, this game still suffers from a lot of the poor game design decisions that starts funneling you into using a guide to actually complete this game. Fortunately, I can say that I didn't run into any of the bugs that were previously reported and I completed the game just fine with a wiki and guide.

If you like playing games very punishing and unforgiving games where you need to consult a wiki/guide to get through it, this game is enjoyable.

If you are extremely OCD to the point where you take screenshots of every screen in your note book and write down every text that you come across, and then you make web graphs of everything like an insane person, then this game is perfect for you.

If you are neither of those things, then stay away from this game.

Pros:
- Most puzzles are clever, mysterious, and the rewards are always fulfilling and interesting.
- Unique style of game play
- Early/mid game is pretty fun

Cons:
- Combat is pretty dry, tedious, uninteresting, repetitive, and awful.
- This game still assumes you write down an insane amount of notes and backtrack throughout the game non-stop.
- This game doesn't suffer as bad as La Mulana 1's translations for puzzles, but the phrasing is still poorly 
translated in context to the puzzles you are trying to solve.
- Often poorly explained puzzles/mechanics.
- Due to all the previous problems, you will get lost, even with a guide because this game obfuscates your goals and a lot of the real information you need to progress. You end up wandering aimlessly and backtracking to rooms that you thought you had already cleared, only to discover through the guide that you weren't supposed to attack some random wall with just your whip, you need "X" to go with it as well. Or some walls being only blown up by certain sub-items, or unlockable with key fairies, etc.

This game has so many good things going for it. The pixel art is amazing, and the in-game sprites are amazing. It has a lot of charm to it. The level design is complex but fun, the enemies are diverse with different patterns to learn, the music has that nice tonality, that makes every area unique, It has a deep and complex lore, and it feels like every single decision you make matters. How many of an item are you going to buy, do you really want to break that wall, are you really going to read that tablet for the second time? SO many decisions and a nonlinear map that feels like you are in Metroidvania Heaven...

So why the negative review? Simple, The Movement is straight up bad. The character feels stiff. It's excessively limited. You can't move in the air unless you jump, changing direction in the air is far too sensitive, but at the same time, limited. Attacking isn't any better, you can only attack what's infront of you, no upward, downward, let alone diagonal attacks. It's such a shame because I really want to continue exploring the game and all the things it has to offer, but subjecting myself to such a slow and annoying movement is so off-putting on an otherwise amazing game. 

The other issue I've found are the boss fights themselves, They've offered almost no challenge, they're dull and drawn out, and are just, overall, not very fun. Then again, these issues are made worse by how bad the movement is. 

Overall, I can only recommend this game if you like great metroidvanias that handle like a bad arcade game.

Final Rating:4.5/10
Not great, definitely not as good as the first. Feels more like you're battling the controls than the game and the puzzles are lacking
