To open the review up I'll answer a simple question: is this game as good as, or even better, than the first? No.

This is a bad game. Somehow, this game takes massive steps backward from the design of the original, a game released in 2005.

The plot of the game doesn't matter; it's just a continuation of the first. You return to the ruins to find an all new one buried deep inside. Like the first, the game is a metroidvania with area-to-area interconnectivity. The graphical and musical direction is the same; however, the ruins of La-Mulana 2 take more influence from Nordic culture, but later there is Hindu influence as well. From a purely aesthetic perspective, this game is as good as the first. In some areas, such as the Gate of the Dead, it surpasses it. There is truly beautiful spritework, beauty that in La-Mulana 1 was saved for back-end areas and the late game. Here, it's everywhere.

So for the gameplay: I suppose the most important aspect of these games is the puzzles. Several other reviewers have pointed out that the puzzles in this game are less cryptic than the first. This is not true. The early game gives this illusion, because for the first part of this game you are actually not solving puzzles at all. You are instead fighting several minibosses, mostly tedious and boring, and often walking from point A to point B. There are many puzzles that are solved by simply talking to an NPC, then talking to another NPC, and now you proceed. The puzzles become important later.

When they do appear, the puzzles are often in the same vein as La-Mulana 1, although more strung out or vague. Some puzzles are elongated by searching for NPCs that magically advance the game, or by having a single puzzle take place in parts of the ruins that are very far apart. Most frustratingly are instances in which you begin a puzzle at an early point in the game and, after searching for a way to solve it, you give up. A very long time later, the solution becomes accessible at a later point. You aren't given the pieces of a puzzle to solve it; you are deprived of a piece and once the game does give it to you, you don't feel satisfied for solving it.

The game has more combat than the first. To compliment this, the controls are more fluid and this can help with quick-paced fights. What's unfortunate is that enemy design is extremely poor. Enemies in this game come in two flavors: they either dash at you (and may be able to jump) or they play keep-away and shoot projectiles at you. I wouldn't say that the enemies are difficult to dispatch. With improved movement you can take out enemies much faster. If this improved movement was placed in the context of the first game, it would be a blast.

The problem is the enemy placement and the world around it. This game has far more enemies per screen than the first game. Despite improved combat, the Castlevania-style knockback has stayed and you will consistently be knocked around from enemy to enemy, stunlocked and unable to escape. Most enemies do not do too much damage, though, so you likely won't be stunlocked until you die. This is where world design comes in. This game has about twice as many holes as the first. The majority of these holes will lead you to spikes, and some will leave you falling for 2-3 screens down without providing you a quick means of ascending to where you fell from. This is especially egregious in Gate of the Dead, where you will often be knocked into holes and go careening down Rube-Goldberg-esque traps likely to hit several spikes and end up a good 10 minute walk from where you fell. With the higher amount of enemies, it isn't an easy matter of avoiding them; if you neglect killing any enemy that could possibly cross your path, you will likely be hit. This can be countered by simply making sure to kill everything, but when so many enemies play keep-away and the rest likely dashing at you to deal some damage before you kill them, this is extremely tedious and unfun. It pointlessly extends playtime and detracts from what should be fun, exploration.

Yet exploration takes the cake for the worst aspect of this game. For a metroidvania, this game counterintuitively punishes the player for deviating from the intended route through the game. Despite being given many directions to take at the start of the game, taking any direction other than what the developers intended will leave you in an incredibly difficult area without the crucial upgrades needed to help you. For example, a mid-game area, Icefire Treetop, is potentially the second area you find, yet it is among the hardest in the game. La-Mulana 1's lava has been replaced with what seems to be poison lava, which will kill you within a second. Add countless enemies that knock you into it and it's extremely unfun to explore. So it begs the question: if the area is so difficult without later upgrades, why let it to be explored in the first place? If you do decide to undertake the area so early, you will not be rewarded with any good items that give you incentive to take the challenge. The entire game is like this; you are allowed to explore areas found later in the game, but they do not bear any rewards. Returning from the first game are the sigils, and this time around, sigils are usually used to prevent the player from accessing treasure in these late-game areas. If you choose to complete a later area early, you will be met with many, many sigil signs that keep you from being rewarded for your effort.

As a quick side note and minor complaint: progression in this game is very slow. The game doesn't reward you very often in general. There is no gratification to solving so many difficult puzzles when doing it only opens a door to the next area. This is amended in the late-game, but it's hard to stay motivated to play that long.

You would think that following the path the developers intended would make the game more enjoyable. No, it isn't. The design of areas in this game are just as linear as the order of the game itself. Instead of areas being interconnected tumbleweeds that are easy and fun to navigate, they are instead more like trees, where moving from one room to another only has a single path (unless you unlock a shortcut, but these are rare.) This makes exploring areas far more slow. Compare the Twin Labyrinths of La-Mulana 1, a large area that was still interconnected and fun to explore, to the equally huge Immortal Battlefield. Despite it's size, each path between each room is linear and thus it's a chore to navigate. Pair this with annoying enemy design and it keeps the game from being fun.

I wanted to save the worst part of this game for last, so I will get to that. This game's levels are designed to be comically unfair. The unfairness of La-Mulana 1's Hell Temple is now the entire game. There are many insta-kill traps that, unlike the first game, have no foreshadowing. Explorations will be ended by an unexpected trap and progress is lost. This isn't hard, it's unfair trial-and-error. When I die I don't blame myself and enjoy learning, the game cheated me. This goes against the hard-but-fair design of La-Mulana 1. The first always made sure that if I died, I only had myself to blame.

I don't see why this sequel was made apart from pleasing fans. The developers didn't expand upon La-Mulana 1. They didn't improve it or top the last. It's just a second helping of the first, but this time there was less thought put into it. Filling the game with insta-kill traps and high amounts of enemies isn't an enjoyable challenge. It's a mimicry of the first game that doesn't capture what made the difficulty rewarding.

Truly awful controls, truly awful monster design, truly awful encounter design. This game is a complete 180 from La Mulana 1. Nigoro learned the complete wrong lessons from that game's success and decided that the best way to challenge the player is to load each area up with shitty mostly invisible death traps, placing save points way out of reach, and making sure each and every screen has monsters that can't be safely engaged or traversed no matter how careful or "skilled" you are.

Lumisa controls like a fucking cripple. Her weapons cannot hit anything below her accept the dagger, which means if you stumble into an enemy they will land 3 or 4 hits on you and bounce you around like a fucking ball. Enemies still do damage even if they're in hit stun so you can't reliably rush through them if you need to. If a monster is blocking your path, 9/10 you have to kill it if you can't completely get around it.

On top of that, Lumisa doesn't have invincibility frames against spikes even when damaged, so if a monster knocks her into spikes, she's fucked.

And to make matters worse, she can't swim for shit. She doesn't sink naturally so you have to hold down while jumping to make her swim down. Except sometimes she just won't swim down, so you take more damage than you really should in water/lava areas. And trying to get out of water is just as much a crap shoot. Sometimes she jumps really high out of water, other times she won't even be able to make a ledge that's right there. Throw in the fucking wall claw item fucking up her attempts at getting out of water and without warning you'll find yourself unable to get out of a water area without taking way more damage than you should.

The levels are laid out such that you have to slog through monsters, many of which have obnoxious movement patterns, react randomly to Lumisa, or move too fast to be safely engaged. Subweapons drop too rarely to be employed, and it doesn't fucking matter because the monsters respawn anyway.

The Frost Giant area was truly the nadir. You need weights just to move around at all times, because the doors do not stay closed and there are a million doors that need to be opened with weights. Why? No fucking reason. No reason at all. Just to waste the player's time and money.

The last encounter I had before I flushed this garbage was against the Squirrel monster in the Ice/Fire Tree. For some fucking reason, the room already has two dangerous and annoying monsters in it, but good luck even getting to that room with anything close to even half health because you have to run a stupid gauntlet of monster-filled rooms, and if you show up at the boss fight with less than half health you might as well go all the way back to the start.

I haven't seen a game try this hard to get the player to quit playing it in a very long time, but congrats Nigoro. A true hack and one-hit-wonder if there ever was one. The amount of stupid buggy controls and tedious level design that got through "quality control" is mind-numbing. I expect this kind of garbage from AAA studios but I see this lack of thoroguh game testing has reached the Japanese small developer scene. Do NOT buy this game whether you liked La Mulana 1 or not.

Terrible jumping mechanics and ridiculous knockback ruin this otherwise fun game. A high level of difficulty can still be achieved without restricting movement, doing so otherwise just feels cheap and frustrating unless the game is balanced fairly around the movement scheme. Additionally, the knockback can cause you to pinball repeatedly into enemy after enemy, making some treks through the levels dangerous and tedious, especially when it causes you to fall several floors below. The monsters will have respawned at that point and you'll have to deal with them again.

I played through the original, freeware version of La-Mulana and had some difficulty then but was otherwise able to finish it. I bought this game hoping some advancements would be made to the gameplay system, instead it's just La-Mulana+.

At first I thought I could work out what to do on my own.  Then I would look up the occasional hint, get a bit further, go exploring on my own - and get my a$$ handed to me. Then I would follow the walkthroughs, get further, go up against tough bosses, somehow defeat them with the awkward controls.  Then I just gave up, since this was not fun.

I loved La-Mulana 1, the controls felt tight, the bosses were difficult but the game was so snappy that it made me feel really good when I learned the fights. And the post game was really fun, not to mention the environments felt like there was a reason or usually a clue when they'd screw you over or when you'd need to teleport to safety.

La Mulana 2 is much more unforgiving than 1, it seems that based on your computers performance and if you look up how to optimize your launch settings, the games movement can feel anywhere from laggy and clunky to slightly delayed, I have not found a way to fully remove the input delay. Even if the bosses were as well designed as in 1, I'd be scared to fight them with controls that feel this bad compared to it's 7 year older predecessor. I've heard about other issues compared to 1 but I can only speak on these issues, I really wanted to enjoy 2 and I'm stuck with it now but while I found 1 to be a masterpiece, 2 is a lackluster sequel that I just want to play due to my love for the first game.

La Mulana 2 is not better than La mulana 1. The first half of La Mulana 2 is better than the first game, but the second half is so much worst. As someone who adores these sorts of games, and has played extensively through La Mulana 1, this game feels like a laugh in the face of the first game, an insult that doesn't stop, puzzles that feel either too insanely easy or too far into the absurdity hard that I'd rather go through gate of illusion again with no guides and my memory wiped, Enemies that are all so frustrating that I want to rip my hair out til I resemble Xelput, and boss fights that feel like a mockery of the original game's bosses in what made them so great, at best this game feels rough, and at worst I am seething mad at the comboing that enemies can do that I'm happily going back to La mulana 1 and drowning myself in my own blood going through Hell temple once more. La mulana 1 was the developers laughing along side the player like a friend showing off a difficult stage they made, La mulana 2 feels more like the developers bashing you over the back of the head as you fall all the way back down gloom because you forgot this ledge was secretly a slope at the edge that you couldnt' do anything about.

The puzzles are fine but the platforming goes beyond being challenging to being obnoxious instead. 

Enemies, traps and platforms are designed and placed to waste your time and resources repeatedly until you can navigate multiple screens in a row perfectly. This would be fine if you only have to go through each obstacle course once, but the amount of backtracking required in this game means you have to go through the same annoyances again and again with increasing difficulty.

Edit: There's one puzzle that is absolutely dumb and I cannot imagine how people are supposedly to figure it out intelligently.

Unlike the first game game, this game is not fun at all. It's not even really about puzzles anymore. It's just a punish platform. The first game had a perfect blend of difficult platforming and brain bending puzzles. This one has brain dead puzzles that are all gated behind tablets and horrible horrible enemy placement with terrible terrible platforming. Feels like the people who made this had no clue why anybody enjoyed anything about the first. I high recommend against this. If you are thinking "I'll just try the second and skip the first" DO NOT DO THAT. Skip the second. Just pretend it doesn't exist and play the first. Be happy it happened and end it there. Another kickstarter failure.

I wish there were a way to have a mixed recommendation, but, as there isn't, this trends more towards the negative side.

Positives first:
+ a very interesting take on multiple separate mythologies. 
+ the puzzles are very good, and not simple push over types of puzzles.
+ as any decent metroidvania, you'll be backtracking all over the place to find new things when you get new powers
+ amazing pixel work. the sprites are very fluid in their movements, and they just look great!
+ very good "other" art (i.e. everything that's not pixel work)

Neutral:
~ The fast travel system, whilst at times frustrating, does have a decent amount of nodes. Time between unlocking those nodes can be a bit long (and those nodes are also the only place to save).
~ the bosses are fairly difficult (as one would expect from a game with the "Souls-like" tag), but some of them are absolute push overs, if you find the right spot to stand/area to move around in; whereas others demand extreme precision to avoid attacks and be able to retaliate. Mostly, tough but fair, some do cross that line to "ok, this is no longer fair, this is straight up bull s**t."

Negatives:
- The movement is kinda jank. So many places that if you get looked at funny by an enemy, you get bounced down four to five screens, and have to *try* to claw your way back up. The control of your character in mid-air is slim to nil.
- It's VERY directionless. Like, once you're out of the first area, you're put into a "Right, here's the world, go find something to do".
- Whilst the puzzles are complex, there are quite a few of them that are VERY obtuse.
- OH HEY LOOK, IT'S AN INSTANT DEATH TRAP OUT OF NO WHERE WITH NO WARNING! Great. There's 20 minutes of platforming and exploration I'm going to have to do again.
- So, so many stupid traps that have no indicator. It's a "git gud" kind of play style, rather than "hey, you've been at this for 20 hours and have figured out the tells for the traps in this area, here's a bunch of other traps with either no tells or tells that you'll only find after the fact"

I did *kind of* enjoy my time with the game. At least enough to put in about 30 hours, but the frustrations I had overcame the joy I had. Rather than some games, where after I beat them, I'm excited for a second play through, or to find a randomizer of them, La-Mulana 2 is one that will go back in the shelf in my game library and likely not be pulled up again. I know there's post-game content, but I just did not enjoy my time enough to go back for it.

And note to people who think the movement in this game is fluid, go try Timespinner. *THAT* is fluid movement.

Making a sequel to a successful game is risky. On one hand, you have the opportunity to expand upon what you had built and fix its issues and shortcomings. But on the other hand, you have the player expectations. Depending on how the sequel is designed, it can fracture its playerbase.
On the surface, La-Mulana 2 seems like a worthy sequel. Areas look really good and characters are more detailed, have smoother animations and sport incredible-looking artworks. Aside from some exceptions like the remixed versions of the first game's tracks, the music still feels pleasant to listen to, even though it's no longer memorable. The controls have also been tweaked and now you are able to correct your position in the air, which makes for some pleasant platforming.
With all that, one is lead to believe that La-Mulana 2 must be nothing but a better version of the first game. But unfortunately, La-Mulana 2 also attempts to change its gameplay formula, turning the end result into a game that maintains a good quality, but diehard fans of its predecessor will have a very hard time enjoying.

[h2]Look how they massacred my boy...[/h2]
I cannot believe how wildly different this game feels compared to the first game. La-Mulana 1 threw you into the gameplay with minimal information and said "good luck" to force you to find everything out for yourself with trial & error, as if you were an archaeologist who was discovering things on their own. La-Mulana 2 however, goes against the design mentality of its prequel especially in the beginning hours.
The first 2-3 hours in La-Mulana 2 has the game deliberately blocking off a lot of pathways to force you to find and beat the first area's boss before doing anything else. If you ever decide to not do that or fail to realize that's what the game wants you to do first, you will be entering the only optionally available area  that features ice physics and instant death hazards, not meant to be messed with at that point. So you're basically forced to do what the game wants you to do before unveiling more of the map or you will get utterly lost and infuriated.
And the situation doesn't get much better after this time period. While the game opens up after beating the first boss and starts to feel more like the first game, it still does things that are quite at odds with what the series originally became known for. For starters, the game puts certain useful items (like the [spoiler]chalice[/spoiler]) directly in your way instead of having you finding them as a reward for exploration or puzzle solving. The progression between areas feels very forced, as if the developers have designed an intended route for you to take, and deviating from this path usually ends with you arriving in locations that have close to zero survival/progression chance as bruteforcing is no longer an option. And then we have the game's newfound love of storytelling.

[h2]Hey! Listen![/h2]
La-Mulana 2 has more emphasis on story and talking with non-playable characters compared to its predecessor. From time to time, you will run into other NPCs in the wild, some of them being key characters that are there for narration reasons, and lots more who you can talk to by entering doors to their chambers. Some of these NPCs only offer various lore tidbits, but there are quite a number of them that have direct influences over the gameplay progression. Not only some of the game's puzzle solutions are bound to doing specific tasks and then talking to specific NPCs for one or multiple times, but the game also blocks access to certain parts of the map and only opens them up after reaching some of these NPCs. Some of the more important ones even send you messages every once in a while to explain how hazards work and tell you where you need to use which items. Coupled with the forced progression path at the beginning of the game, and all of the other changes, these make for a more controlled experience compared to the first game. 
And all of this can underwhelm the fans of the previous installment, to the point I was seriously considering getting a refund due to how awful and streamlined the experience felt for me. All of these new design decisions go against the groundwork laid by the first game. No longer you are finding about things by yourself and no longer the hurdles that block the way to new areas are your wits and your equipment. Speaking of which...

[h2]Why does it feel like I've accomplished nothing so far?[/h2]
Progression in La-Mulana 2 feels painfully slow and unrewarding, and you will probably be shocked (in a negative way) to find out how much stuff you have found on your own after a couple hours of adventuring.
After 6 hours in La-Mulana 1, half of my inventory was filled with items that each helped me progress further in the game. I was constantly finding new items to use and in turn getting access to new locations. Then I play La-Mulana 2 and after 8 hours of gameplay resulting in the discovery of 8 fast travel locations and slaying two bosses, I still feel like I have done nothing of value as my inventory is nearly empty. The game conveniently puts important items in your way instead of asking you to find them in the wild, and then it has the nerve to act stingy when it comes to rewarding you when you actually put in some effort. Many times you solve puzzles just to see pathways opening instead of getting a reward or beat minibosses/bosses to get items that you either don't need at the time or don't know what to do with them. To put a cherry on top of everything, many of the chests are now locked behind sigils instead of puzzles so you won't be rewarded for trying to attempt a later area earlier.

[h2]One step forward, two steps back...[/h2]
And that's just the changes to exploration. When it comes to combat, La-Mulana 2 is also not completely satisfactory. The improved controls do make for a nicer time going around and fighting with the enemies and bosses, but I do not understand the decision to reduce the invulnerability time. There are a lot of places in the game where you can get stunlocked by the enemies and traps. You get hit by an enemy, get knocked backwards as a result, then hit another enemy/projectile/trap and take another hit as the invulnerability time ends quickly. This is especially visible with the enemies who carry weapons that act like semi-automatic guns.
And then we have the bosses and minibosses who are boring and not fun to fight at all this time around. Many of the bosses require only the bare minimum of your platforming abilities. If you are especially attentive and lucky, you might even find flaws in their behavior and make some of them freeze in place, not moving at all and ready to take hits. There is alot to like with this game. And I there is alot I do like about the game. But ultimately I do not recommend it. Only stubborn pride has carried me through the last 8 hours and I am at my breaking point. This game is not for casual fun. This is not a test of skill or dexterity. It is a test of patience and endurance. And I feel it a damn shame that a game this pretty and vast, in a genre I love, only frustrates me. 

As far as I can tell there seems to have been little to no change in mechanics from La Mulana 1. It is just bigger and more confusing and the first one was big and confusing to begin with. 

Sprite work is gorgeous. The environments feel larger than life and there is a great sense of exploring. The controls are not the best but have certain quality that takes some getting used to. This feels like a labour of love by passionate people. It is grand and fantastic. But all the good things also come with fairly major problems. The graphics are so detailed that things that need to stand out are lost in the noise. Looking at you, pressure plates and tiny buttons. The large environments are easy to get lost in and there are dead ends and weird puzzles everywhere. And the initial sense of wonder at exploration is soon replaced with tedium because this game has no sense of flow or direction at all. It seems to actively delight in opening up areas that are too high level or that instantly reveal themselves to need a specific item or mantra or app or something.
And to get through this game without the aid of a walkthrough requires psychotic levels of patience and dedication. I took notes until my notes need to be structured and color coded because finding things in my own notes took more time than the game. 

And this game is hard. Git Gud kind of Hard. Hard with hard R. And hard games can be fun. But this feels more like "I Wanna Be The Guy" than "Dark Souls". The vast, vast, vast majority of my deaths were due to instant death traps. The rest from being serial bodied and comboed into spikes repeatedly. No boss has taken more than 4 or 5 tries. And the harder "bosses" are more annoying than hard. There is no real test of skill. Just remember the patterns. You'll find a loop and then it just feels like cheesing. The glacial pace for killing the bosses without risking anything is another pain and brings no satisfaction because "Cool, now I get to be lost for another couple of hours while retreading every inch of the map." If the controls were tighter or more precise and you could control you jump better most of the frustration would be gone. But it is so easy to be hit and be flung down a pit into more enemies and spikes.

Which brings us to just navigating from screen to screen. No one room is seldom brutal though there are some. Even the somewhat clunky controls start to feel good once you get used to the. Each room CAN be navigated without even risking much damage. But it is boring. Most enemies have way more health than is needed. Clearing a room takes forever. And even then if you fail and fall out of the room there is a chance enemies will respawn. But it can still be fun. 

The frustration starts to build because you have no idea where you are supposed to go and no indication of where to go in the sprawling maze rife with many very specific circuitous routes that span 8 different biomes. And because the Warp Points are so far apart you have to back track ALOT and chances are that when you finally find where you need to be you will be so damaged that you need to heal which means you have to go back to town and then do the treck again. Only to die to some instant death trap almost instantly. 

The fun of exploration and combat is completely eclipsed by the tedium and frustration of navigation through the environments.

Which is sort of where I am at. Just frustrated. All the good will has been whittled away. Because if you are not constantly and highly vigilant at all times it is super easy to get hurt, get lost and sometimes even stuck, so you have to warp back and try again. And this wouldn't be a huge problem if the save points were just a little more frequent.

I can forgive the death traps, the back tracking and even the lack of some linear progression help. Even the clunky handling of the character is fine in the grand scheme. But many tiny annoyances have just drained the fun away. And when I got the slippery ice level I gave up. I may very well not return. It is hard to pinpoint exactly when in the progression I started to get fed up because I have no clue how far I have progressed. Since many of the seemingly Key Items never have been used. 

But I think I can sum up the critical point: 

When instant or near instant death becomes the rule and not the exception. 


-Final thoughts

This game is not for everyone. Some may love it because it is so frustrating. I imagine I might finish it (with the aid of a guide) just to say that I did it. It is a thing to overcome and enjoy only in retrospect. For I am not having fun.

La-Mulana 2 is a sequel to La-Mulana, a side-scrolling exploration and puzzle solving platformer, and is in the same vein as it's predecessor.

The game requires the player to locate and solve a variety of secrets within a sprawling ruins, only sometimes through cryptic clues given through text written on tablets scattered around the ruins. All the while, the player must fight through swarms of monsters as they travel from room to room, and occasionally face off against tougher foes in order to gain additional clues or items vital to the player's success.

This game, just like it's prequel, creates a hostile and repulsive experience for just about any player in a way that can easily make the game impossible for them.

Most importantly, the game doesn't give the player an expectation for the types of puzzles they will have to solve. There are some secret walls, some floor switches, but the exact approach to solving some of the puzzles in the game have absolutely no introduction, or uselessly poor hints to them. This makes it so that, no matter how long one plays the game, they may never beat it, ever, as it would be impossible to guarantee that a player explores every possible puzzle solution that the developers could program into the game. One's intuition when solving a puzzle could lead them astray in potentially dozens of different ways even if every clue was placed in front of them.

Even beyond that, many hints were poor, or deliberately difficult to access, which is not enjoyable. Even La-Mulana had a more focused set of puzzles, with only a couple notable instances violating reasonability, whereas in La-Mulana 2, the game often refuses to meet you halfway, requiring you to interact with the invisible or impossibly obscure by perfectly deciphering easily misconstrued hints. It goes without saying that this game is light years more difficult than it's prequel, La-Mulana, as a complete start-to-finish playthrough without any hints, due it's eccentric range of puzzle abstraction.

That is to say nothing of the combat, which through the increased fluidity of movement, both of the player and enemy, only succeeded in becoming more manic. Enemy density, attack speed, and attack flexibility only increased, while the duration of invulnerability the player gets after being hit was significantly reduced. The player's movement was improved, particularly movement while in the air, but it was a small change in comparison to the vast increase in franticness applied to just about every room in the game.

The graphics increased in resolution, a large variety of interesting characters to talk to were added, and a mostly new story premise was invented for La-Mulana 2, but for the most part, this game feels poorly tuned despite it's surface level polish. Though I hated La-Mulana as a whole, I respected it greatly in parts. I can say nothing of the sort for La-Mulana 2.

At the same time, the openness of the game has started working against it, because I'll fight my way through a tough section, only to be "rewarded" with a room where I have to use an item that I haven't found yet.

Mulana 1 was 30 hours long, and I think that would've been the perfect length for Mulana 2 as well (the average "how long to beat" listed here on Steam is 47 hours). I'm getting close to 40 hours of this second playthrough, and the game has worn out its welcome with same-y areas full of uninspired enemies and platforming, while giving up completely on clever puzzles, replacing them with nonsensical puzzles that can only be solved with trial and error, and "challenges" with obvious solutions that are just a huge chore to do.

Don't play this game, it feels like a waste of time. If you explore the map you will get very confused about the puzzles, some of the solutions to the puzzles are found in totally different parts of the map and mostly amount to using the right item in a room. There were a few clever puzzles that were fun but most of  the time its just stuff that makes you use a guide. Even with a guide to the puzzles its still confusing.
One step forward, two steps back. That's all.

A lot harder than La-Mulana 1. Uses high density of enemies to create difficulty, which feels cheap and unfair. La-mulana 2 is actively hostle to the player in ways La-mulana 1 wasn't. Even if you don't activate hard mode, player progress will create the same effect once half of the levels are completed. Maybe you will like that but you should know that the first few levels are not representative of the rest of the game.

La-Mulana 2 is as much fun as the first one, but I can't recommend it in its current state. The game is extremely buggy and should be marked as Beta or Early Access. There are minor bugs like crashes when loading saves or getting stuck in walls, but also a ton of game breaking bugs that can make your save file unwinnable. Basic things like using the Holy Grail in some rooms or bringing fairies can break your progress. If you fail to find a hidden character in time you can no longer win. The translation is also pretty bad at times and some hints are completely mistranslated. There are a lot of examples like this in the Bug Report thread and I've also run into a couple myself. If you decide to buy it right now, then make sure to use a new save slot every couple hours, so you can at least go back if something breaks.

La-Mulana 2 is a true sequel to the first game. It picks up where the story ended and borrows a lot of items and early game locations from it. The controls aren't as stiff anymore, which is a nice change, but you still have to jump with care. The music is as good as ever and the character portraits are gorgeous. There is a lot of content in this game. So far the puzzles haven't been as cryptic as in the previous game, but that might change for the end game riddles. It still feels very rewarding to solve a room and get an item that will unlock even more areas and puzzles. Boss fights are pretty easy if you use everything the game offers, but that was also an option in the first game with the gun.

Overall I'm having a ton of fun exploring La-Mualana 2, but I would strongly recommend waiting until the major bugs get fixed.

I really liked the first game, so I bought this as soon as it came out. You should definitely wait.

Between game-breaking bugs and bad translations that make puzzles essentially impossible to solve, the game is simply broken.

I fought one boss that jumped out of the screen and disappeared. Another boss right after that lunged to attack and froze in place. In both cases, I was stuck - I couldn't kill the boss, and had to reload the game.

I also ran into a case where the game locked up when I tried to enter a doorway - the character went into the animation of entering the door, but the game got stuck, and again I had to reload.

One puzzle in particular is flat out broken because of poor translation. I only managed to progress by reading how to solve it in the forums from someone who played the Japanese version. Apparently, an essential clue is left out.

I really want to like this game, but I've reloaded my same save nearly 30 times now, and I am held back by bugs that force me to reload. I might revisit the game later, after it gets some significant updates.

I do not recommend for numerous design decisions, but I will start with positives.

+ A phenomenal soundtrack. The updated soundtrack is great.
+ Story starts really strong. There are many interesting answers to archaeology, mythology and established lore. Also, the game holds many characters to talk with. However, I wish we understood how these people sustained themselves in the ruins. They lack food and the water is poisonous.
+ Game mechanics and tools mostly improved, but also degraded in some ways. Spaulder, Chakram and Earth Spear are fantastic. Mantras are brought in early to diversify puzzle-solving. But the original slower pace is removed with easy ladder movement and few intrusive objects of divine punishment. Jumping is also less organic and makes platforming less fun to me. Enemy knockback seems increased in general and some have extra knockback, which would be fine if spikes were not upgraded to ignore invincibility and do insane damage.
+ Deviates from the Guardian and Area themes like frontside and backside dungeons. Refreshing.
+ Guardian fights are really fun, diverse and a lot more manageable in most cases. Mini-bosses can be a different story with later ones being occasional nonsense without sub-weapons.
+ An item gives weapons new meaning. Weapons that start out underpowered can become invaluable.

That should be every positive. A lot of subtle things feel inferior. Maps are bigger to their detriment because the Feather fails to be useful in exploration and everything feels less engaging. It is usually for jumping out of a fall rather than reaching higher places. Ironically, the game scales difficulty based on your progress, leading to more and new enemies to populate every room. Most painful are skeletons, which not only are less easy to differentiate, but also are often blue skeletons that make the game frustrating for no reason. It takes many hours before you can get their weakness and you probably will not face many after getting the upgrade anyway. Additionally, bosses increase in HP and damage. I explored much out of order. By the time I fought the 3rd guardian Kujata, it felt like a final boss and I imagine most players quitting there.

I will explain why I fell out of order. Many hints have issues. The English is far more plain than La-Mulana 1, but the philosophy has become disorienting. In Annwfn are two treasures I had desperately needed, but missed until about 20 hours in. I had explored more than 10 different areas, but only received life upgrades, maps and crystal skulls, as well as glossary entries (which are a really bad secret. Like Shin Megami Tensei V essences, they ruin the feelings of discovery and improvement by gathering many items that rarely benefit you.). It had dissatisfied me and felt unwise to open so many areas from the start. La-Mulana 1 is a non-linear game, but it is hard to miss out on the most essential items to solve puzzles in new areas if you do branch out. But in La-Mulana 2, you are punished for wandering and you find nothing. All could have been remedied if hint tablets did not gloss over the most vital items. They give multiple hints on some very obvious puzzles; actually inducing confusion. For example, a puzzle in Shrine of the Frost Giants tells you to fill in a pillar. There are TWO tablets for this, but I beat the game without finding what is meant by this. I thought I had made progress on the puzzle, until I had checked the initial state of the area and saw no difference. In the end, it likely hinted toward a breakable wall, which is illogical.

I present another problem. This game has gone through a lot of weird patches which cause hints and other elements of the game to become irrelevant. For example, I had thought I found an unintentional puzzle solution in Roots of Yggdrasil. I have learned that I did it correctly, but the puzzle seems to rely on stopping time. In fact, stopping time is hinted at WAY TOO EARLY, so I had begun thinking I access it earlier than in La-Mulana 1. This belief had caused SO MUCH PAIN. The Time Lamp takes LONGER to get than in La-Mulana 1. I had hoped they would introduce it earlier, as with the mantras. But instead, the early Time Lamp recharge stations are distractions. There are many recharge stations, yet no one would suffer with having only TWO. Time Lamp is necessary only two or three times, but the area design implies you need it many times.

Another reckless decision is naming an area Buried Fortress after there are references to digging into an entirely different nearby area. This had me miss vital clues for a long time as I focused on a whole area, not a room.  And this is a super important item. I had to look at a guide or I would almost never have found the solution. Something very direct in theory becomes really disorienting with sloppy use of related words.

What started getting really inconsistent is writing, which really started dissipating mid- to late-game. Even during the most climactic story moments, character dialogue stagnates, even in main characters. Before the mid-point of the game, numerous dialogue changes happen. You can even find premature hints that should have been spread later. Some side characters also ignore events regarding them. For example, you meet Eurydice’s lover, but after meeting with Eurydice and solving her problem, the lover’s dialogue is unchanged. There are also characters with scant meaning in a game where talking to an NPC can be vital, which discourages you from a good behavior you develop. In fact, many NPCs in harder to reach areas do not say anything valuable.

Also worth noting that end-game songs are really messy. The last three songs pale in comparison to those in La-Mulana 1, which includes the final boss theme. Previous Guardians have many of the greatest songs.

The Guardian doors get annoying, but they also existed in the first game, more subtly. It stinks that every Guardian feels important with doors and treasures they open, but later become almost meaningless. It goes from [spoiler]5 souls to 9 [/spoiler] with nothing to open in between. No 5 soul doors give anything truly valuable, which again ruins the value of exploration. And the treasures past 5 souls also get meaningless.

Oh, and you may hope to influence the plot, but the only scene meaningful in this way prevents a logical solution from applying, which frustrates and cheapens the plot surrounding that character. Also, there are two secret bosses, but they only provide extra glossary entries with little to say.

 [spoiler] Ancient Chaos and Dark Star Lord’s Mausoleum[/spoiler] waste what seem like something to dispel by solving certain puzzles. They serve no purpose than being generic holy relics.

Lastly, this game draws from its predecessor too much. Many refreshing concepts are possible, but instead 80% of your possessions match the first game. Only one new weapon, and garb and item which act like more. The main weapons lose meaning too, since almost nothing requires specific weapons to open.

Lots of tediuous running around because you are limited on how many clues you can carry. I really enjoyed the level design but that was about it. There are a lot of bosses but most of them could be cheesed because of the broken AI. Like if I happen to be standing in a certain spot where I could just keep hitting them and they couldn't attack me. They added a lot more smaller enemies too but it's not difficult or fun combat, they just make running from room to room a nuisance while hunting for clues.

Note: I finished the game, this is a negative review purely because there is no thumbs-sideways mixed option.

For every thing La-Mulana 2 does right it also does a couple things wrong. For example, widescreen rooms - that's nice, but why are there jpeg borders ALL AROUND the screen? Just let me play it in actual fullscreen, like the first game did. Or, more bosses - that's cool, but why do they repeat and why can they be cheesed so easily? You shouldn't let the player get away with getting a boss stuck on a tiny platform and throwing fifty shurikens at their face, like the first game did. Or, better mobility - that's great, but why do I constantly find myself jumping ahead to actual dead-ends that are opened only by progress on the apparent intended route? First game did it better, whatever, you get it.

What were they thinking?!

Really, my last point is probably the most damning one - the game holds your hand so much in the first half and expects you to make repeat visits to NPCs (which happened exactly twice in La-Mulana 1 and at least made sense) that you forget how to think for yourself. Oh, I don't see a solution in the next room, so I better go make the rounds! Oh ♥♥♥♥ off.

If you dare to go off route by, let's say, throwing fifty shurikens at Nidhogg (and then some of them will phase through his hitbox and deal no damage, who knows why), the first boss you're obviuosly meant to fight later, you get a grapple claw that doesn't really get you anywhere at that point, about two hundred coins to spend on nothing of note except for an item that shows boss HP, and a location full of frustrating near-instant kill traps and dead-ends.

And then you find out that the item straight up just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ lies to you about boss HP, because first the bar has to change color several times before it starts going down, so you can clearly see that you're doing damage but never know how much until the end of the fight.

This is just the first major instance of this, but now I've seen it come up in several reviews and let me tell you, I understand their frustration. It keeps happening again and again. You will be left scratching your head because you will keep finding locations where something is supposed to happen, but LATER, pay them no mind and go progress the intended route!

Learning to shut my somewhat genre-savvy gamer brain off that tells me to check off the beaten path left me holding the bag when the game STOPPED literally nudging me towards the end. I still have no idea how you're supposed to collate the actual solution to the Dark Star Lord puzzles, for example, because I just seemingly brute-forced them.

All in all, it's a swing and a miss, but if they ever come up with a third game I’ll make sure to check it out, I only hope they forget to bring the guy responsible for the first half of La-Mulana 2.

I may not have a state-of-the-art gaming PC, but this is a 2d, flip-screen platformer with pixel graphics. How is it possible for it to be so badly optimized that it runs slowly even at minimum graphics settings?

On top of that, there are currently game-breaking (as in "you have to start over from the beginning") bugs that the dev team have shown no interest in fixing.

I love La-Mulana, there's no denying that. But La-Mulana 2 is disappointing in many ways. Although there were a lot of new innovations, the localization is sort of prejudiced at parts, and the game is absolutely riddled with bugs, some of which are completely game-stopping and don't show up until you're 90% of the way through the game. They introduced a major softlock bug in the game on November 21st, and 80 days later it's still here. It's not the first time, either. A few weeks after the game launched there was a boss which refused to die, the Griffin, due to another mispatch. That one was fixed a week later, but it really soured the game for a lot of players.

The bosses at launch ranged from absurd to bugged to insta-murdery. Many of those have since been patched.

The story retcons a lot of the ideas and relationships behind the first game, and kind of undoes some of the mystery that made the first game a success.

It is a shame what became of this game. I'm sorry I invested as much time in it as I have.

I cannot recommend you purchase this game, because it will only reinforce careless behavior for the developers. Stop coddling them, please. They are adults, do not reward them when they do bad things.

Limited action cancelling means you will get stuck in attack animations all the time.  Combat is simply not satisfying.  The first hours of the game are pretty good.  You solve a puzzle, you get a new weapon or power, and you metroidvania your way to new areas, weapons, and powers.  As the game progresses, though, the puzzles become (in my opinion) too challenging and inscrutible, and there are too many insta-death traps.  As you progress through the game the number of enemies ramps up to the point where it's very annoying to simply walk through the game's levels.   There are improvements here over La-Mulana 1, but I still want to see a more modern take on this franchise with better combat and more accessibility overall.

La Mulana 2, and its predecessor are an excellent idea for a game, but they are both very flawed in their execution.

Both games are much too obtuse for their own good, and follow that up by shooting themselves in the foot when it comes to their difficulty design. La-Mulana 2 does this worse than the original.

Some things are poorly designed to the point that you will not find them without a guide. In fact, a guide is pretty much required unless you want to possibly be in the ruins for the rest of your real life. Character movement is better than in the original, but still wonky.

Some boss battles are very cheap and unfair. The game also has many areas where you can get screwed over by the excessive knockback. For example, it’s very annoying when an enemy inevitably knocks you down a hole, sometimes sending you plummeting several screens before landing on something. This then means you have a long walk ahead of you just to get back to where you were. So yea, the level design is cheap in some spots as well.

While La-Mulana 2 is a great idea for a game, it’s definitely not one of the best Metroidvania's out there.

I wish I could recommend La-Mulana 2.  I really do.  Even though a boss I couldn't master stopped me from finishing the first one, it is one of my all time favourite games.  For a large portion of La-Mulana 2, it was looking to be going the same way.  But then, too many bugs, a ridiculous stun-lock, a bad translation making many puzzles make literally no sense in english, and too many troll-deathtraps, and all the fun was sucked out of it.

I thought seriously about quitting during the Halls of Malice.  I genuinely quit when in Nibiru, and Mjolnir simply would not work the way it was supposed to.  I'm not saying anything else so as to not spoil anything for other users; I'm mentioning those two things so that if you do buy it you'll understand why I cannot recommend it even though I absolutely adore La-Mulana's world, and most of the time I've spent in it.  

I'm absolutely gutted if I'm honest, moreso than I can say I've been with a game in years.

Unfortunately I have to warn against this game. The first one was one of my favorite platformers but the devs seem to have completely missed what actually made that one fun. It wasn't constant infuriating enemy and trap setups that just make it tedious to even attempt to explore. It also wasn't constant information overload that lead to you just constantly retreading the entire available game for the one single thing you overlooked in the hopes of making slight progress only to immediately hit another dead end and have to repeat the process. That [i]was[/i] an issue in the first one, just not to this degree. (It was acceptable there because it was in moderation.) And when you finally found that one thing you overlooked it didn't typically result in another nearly instant roadblock.

It's rare for a game to make me hate a field more than Hell Temple from the first game but it's even rarer for the same game to succeed at that task again later on. (And this is coming form someone who actually largely enjoyed Hell Temple other than that one vertical spike room.)


Edit: As an addendum after having reached the final area of the game, it only gets worse. There's not only one field worse than the one I'd previously mentioned but the final area is literally Hell Temple Redux: Let's See How Big of Jerks We Can Be To Our Players. It's largely an okay area other than some annoying miniboss refights. But then you hit the Annoying Room of Kaizo Spike Bullshìttery™ pt. II where this time if you hit one spike you hit EVERY spike on that side of the spike pit then fall into a room where you're forced to refight a fairly tough miniboss, who can instantly kill you if you're not careful, just to retry the spike room again. And this room is not optional unlike the equivalent room in Hell Temple. This is a required room to even complete the game.

At this point I'm not even bothering to finish the game despite having stubbornly gotten nearly 100% completion (other than one glossary entry which I learned about after getting its location completely locked off) despite my previous complaints about the game. It feels like Nigoro took the least fun bits of the first game and focused on those while polishing up the actual game mechanics themselves.
Yeah... I don't know about this one.  There were some patches that happened post-release and you can just tell they weren't play tested.
